passages.title: Case File Zero: Before the First City
passages.text:
The Provenance Office keeps one promise.  Nothing gets filed as fact until the evidence proves it.  Old claims drift as time passes.  Conquerors rewrite the past to look better.  Rivals erase what came before them.  Forgers invent whole records from nothing.  A new field Recorder's first job is simple.  Open the oldest case in the whole record, and find where solid ground begins.

For most of human history, people moved with the seasons, living in small bands and hunting and gathering wild food.  No single place could feed a group for long, so nobody built anything meant to last.  Then, in a few river valleys, people learned a new trick.  They planted seeds on purpose and waited for a harvest.  Farming grew more food than hunting ever had, and extra food let some people stop searching for their next meal.  They settled down instead, and villages grew into towns.  Some towns grew large enough to become the first cities.

Two rivers explain why the first cities rose where they did.  In Mesopotamia, the Tigris and the Euphrates flooded every year, spreading fresh soil across the land nearby.  That soil grew far more food than dry ground could.  The floods were hard to predict, though, coming early some years and late in others.  Managing that water took real teamwork, canals, walls, and shared rules.  Farther west, the Nile flooded on a far steadier yearly schedule, so Egyptian farmers could plan around it.  Deserts on both sides of the Nile kept most invaders away, and a steadier, safer valley let Egypt unite sooner.

Both rivers prove the same rule the Office repeats to every new Recorder.  Geography decided where a civilization could begin.  What people built next is where the record gets interesting.

passages.title: Recovered Entry: The Code of Hammurabi
passages.text:
This entry gathers the Provenance Office's own working translation.  It covers several clauses from the law code of Hammurabi.  Hammurabi was a king of Babylon in ancient Mesopotamia.  The stone the code was carved on still exists.  Nothing here is a forgery.  The dispute is not whether the code is real.  The dispute is what the code actually did for the people living under it.

The code's own opening lines state its purpose plainly.  Its laws exist so that a strong man cannot crush a weak one.  They exist so that a widow or an orphan can get a fair hearing.  Read alone, that sounds like protection for the whole kingdom equally.

The clauses that follow tell a more complicated story.  One clause covers a man of high standing who destroys another man's eye.  If the victim holds the same high standing, the attacker's own eye is destroyed in return.  A second clause covers that very same injury done to a man of common standing.  It orders a payment of silver instead of a matching injury.  A third clause covers that same injury done to an enslaved person.  It sets the payment lower still, at half the enslaved person's own value, paid to that person's owner.  The punishment changes with the victim's standing.  The injury itself never changes at all.

Other surviving clauses cover house builders, merchants, and farmers.  Most of them share this same pattern.  A careless builder whose work kills a house owner is put to death.  That same builder's careless work, if it only kills the owner's enslaved worker, costs him a replacement instead.

The Provenance Office files this entry as verified but unresolved.  The code's opening promise and its actual clauses do not fully agree.  Did Hammurabi mean to protect ordinary people?  Or did he mainly mean to keep each rank of society fixed in its place?  That is the real question every Recorder assigned to this case has to weigh.

passages.title: Case File: Two Kingdoms of the Nile
passages.text:
Egyptians believed their king, the pharaoh, was not an ordinary ruler.  They believed he held a kind of divine power.  His main job was keeping the whole world in balance, a balance Egyptians called ma'at.  Two pharaohs left a large mark on the record.  Hatshepsut ruled Egypt in her own right as a full pharaoh, not merely as a king's wife.  She sent a famous trading trip south along the coast.  Years later, Ramses the Second reigned for decades and built huge monuments.  He later signed one of the oldest peace deals in the whole record.

Religion shaped how Egyptians treated their own dead.  Egyptians believed a spirit needed a preserved body to survive into the next life, so skilled workers made mummies to stop a body from decaying.  Wealthier Egyptians built large tombs and filled them with goods the dead were thought to need on the trip ahead.  That belief is the real reason the pyramids exist at all.

South of Egypt, along the same river, sat the kingdom of Kush.  Egypt and Kush traded gold, ivory, and other goods for centuries, but their bond was never simply friendly.  Egypt's own armies took over Kush during Egypt's strongest era.  Years later, that balance flipped.  Kushite kings conquered Egypt itself and ruled it as pharaohs in their own right, keeping many Egyptian customs alongside their own.

The two peoples even wrote their history in different ways.  Mesopotamian scribes pressed wedge-shaped cuneiform marks into wet clay, using a cut reed, one tablet at a time.  Egyptian scribes instead drew or carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone, a system built from hundreds of small pictures.  Both systems did the same basic job.  They let a record live on long after its maker was gone.

passages.title: Case File: A Covenant Without a Kingdom Yet
passages.text:
Most peoples in the old Near East worshipped many gods at once.  The Hebrew Bible describes something different taking root among a group later known as the Israelites.  It describes Abraham as the first to promise loyalty to one God alone.  In exchange, that account describes a covenant, a solemn promise of land and heirs.  That one choice is the seed of monotheism, the belief in exactly one God.  This whole file keeps coming back to that belief.

The Hebrew Bible next tells of years spent in Egypt.  Abraham's heirs became slaves there, under an Egyptian king.  It tells of Moses leading them out of that slavery.  That event is remembered as the Exodus.  At Mount Sinai, tradition holds that Moses got a code of law for his people to live by.  It renewed the same covenant Abraham had made years before.

After reaching the land of Canaan, judges first led the Israelites, called on only when trouble struck.  Later, the Israelites chose kings instead.  Saul became the first.  David, the second, united the tribes more firmly and made Jerusalem his capital.  David's son Solomon built the First Temple there, one central place for the tradition's most sacred rites.

For years after Solomon, three things stood as one.  A king ruled.  A Temple centered worship.  A covenant explained why both stood at all.  The Office's next entry tests exactly how strong that link really was.  Outside armies later tore two of those three things away.

passages.title: Case File: The Shortest File Outlasts Its Own Temple
passages.text:
This case file is the shortest one in the whole Office archive.  That is exactly what makes it worth checking closely.  A tradition without a king, a Temple, or a homeland of its own should have simply faded away.  It should have faded into the peoples around it.  The record shows it did not.

The first blow came when the Babylonian army conquered the kingdom of Judah.  The army destroyed the First Temple in Jerusalem and forced many Israelites into exile, far from their own land.  That exile is remembered as the diaspora.  It grew as more people scattered even further from home over later years.  Years later, Persian rulers let the exiles return and build a Second Temple on that same site.

The Second Temple stood for centuries.  Then a Roman army destroyed it too, during a revolt long after Israel's old kings had reigned.  This second loss should have finished the tradition for good.  Rome had already crushed the state.  Now the Temple, the tradition's central home, was gone too.

The record credits a teacher named Yohanan ben Zakkai with the turn that followed.  Tradition holds that he escaped the besieged city.  He got permission from Roman rulers to open a small school in a town called Yavneh.  Teaching there, without any Temple at all, he changed the tradition's whole center of gravity.  Priests had once made offerings in one sacred building.  Now study, prayer, and law took that place, and any group could carry those things with it, anywhere.

That shift is the real claim behind this file's short length, now fully checked.  The tradition outlived its own state and its own Temple.  It did not rebuild either one.  It proved instead that it had never truly leaned on them alone.

passages.title: Source A: The Athenian Account, Filed by the Aegean Desk
passages.text:
Greece's own land decided its shape long before any war began.  Mountains cut the land into small, separate pockets, and the sea reached almost every one of them.  No single valley could feed a kingdom big enough to rule the whole region.  Instead, dozens of separate city-states grew up.  Each one ran its own government.  Each one guarded its own coast.

Athens took its own government further than most cities dared.  Its assembly let adult male citizens vote directly on the city's laws.  This system is remembered as democracy, rule by the people themselves.  Enslaved people, foreigners, and women could not vote.  The system's real reach was smaller than the word alone suggests.  Still, within that limited group, Athens gave plain citizens a truly direct voice.  A culture built on open debate grew up alongside it.  A thinker named Socrates walked the city asking sharp questions.  His questions made easy ideas fall apart in public.

The Persian Empire invaded Greece twice.  Athens filed its own account of what really won the war.  Athenian soldiers stood almost alone at Marathon.  They turned back the first Persian invasion outright.  Years later, an even bigger force arrived.  Athens poured newly found silver into a huge navy.  The leader Themistocles pushed hard for this plan.  At Salamis, that navy trapped the Persian fleet in a narrow strait.  It wrecked the fleet outright.  The invasion's push broke for good.  The Persian king pulled back with most of his army.

This account does not deny that other cities fought bravely too.  It simply argues that ships, not soldiers, won the war.  A closing note from the Aegean Desk adds one more point.  Greek ways did not stay locked inside these city-states forever.  A Macedonian king named Alexander later carried them across a much wider empire.

passages.title: Source B: The Spartan-Leaning Account, Filed by the Peloponnese Desk
passages.text:
Sparta's own account of the Persian Wars starts with its government.  That government looked nothing like Athens.  Two kings ruled Sparta at once, checking each other's power.  A council of elders helped run the city.  A small board of overseers, called ephors, ran its daily business.  Plain citizens still met in an assembly.  Real power sat with a much smaller, older group than Athens ever let near its own choices.

Spartan life itself was built around one goal.  Every Spartan boy entered a harsh army training system at a young age.  He stayed a soldier his whole adult life.  A large group of unfree workers, called helots, farmed the land instead.  This let Spartan citizens stay in training at all times.  Sparta's government existed to keep that one army ready.  This account argues that readiness is exactly what saved Greece when Persia invaded.

The second Persian invasion arrived, and this file credits Sparta with the war's real turning points.  King Leonidas led a small, Spartan-led force.  His force held a narrow mountain pass at Thermopylae.  The Persian army there was many times its size.  The stand ended in defeat, but it bought Greece precious time.  It became a lasting sign of resistance.  The next year, an allied Greek army met the last Persian force on open ground at Plataea.  A Spartan leader led that army.  It beat the Persians outright.  The invasion was finally driven out of Greece for good.

This account treats the earlier sea battle at Salamis in a different way.  It calls Salamis one useful step among several, not the single moment that decided everything.  Two files, filed by two different desks, tell of the very same war.  The Office keeps both.  It refuses to force one account to lose.

passages.title: Case File: The Quiet Record of the Indus
passages.text:
Some files in the Office archive are quiet for a reason.  Nothing bad happened; the people involved simply cannot speak for themselves yet.  The Indus Valley civilization built some of the best-planned cities anywhere in the old world.  Mohenjo-daro and Harappa sat on careful grids.  Baked-brick homes linked to covered drains, an advanced setup for its time.

The Indus people also left behind a written script.  It was cut into thousands of small stone seals.  No scholar has ever managed to read it.  Every other early society in this record can be read straight, in its own words.  Court records, temple writings, and trader letters survive elsewhere.  The Indus people left none of that.  Whatever its people believed, ruled, or argued about stays locked behind an unread script.  This file treats that gap honestly instead of guessing past it.

Its fall is easier to weigh, though still not fully settled.  The clearest evidence involves shifting rivers.  One major stream that once fed Indus farms seems to have dried up or changed path.  Evidence also points to a weaker monsoon.  That means longer, harsher dry spells across the region.  Farming likely grew far harder to keep up.  Many of the biggest cities emptied out slowly, not all at once.  Scholars still argue over how much of the fall came from nature alone.

Sometime after the Indus cities faded, new migrants arrived from the northwest.  Many scholars think these Indo-Aryan migrants brought an early form of Sanskrit with them.  They brought a new set of faith practices too.  Those practices were set down in hymns called the Vedas.  The Vedas became the base the next file builds right on top of.

passages.title: Case File: Dharma, the Buddha, and an Emperor's Change of Heart
passages.text:
Many scholars think Vedic hymns arrived with the Indo-Aryan migrants.  Over time, they grew into a much larger faith, the one now known as Hinduism.  Hindus came to believe in dharma, a person's proper duty in life.  They also came to believe in karma, the belief that every act carries results that follow a person forward.  Vedic life also split into four broad groups, called varnas.  Birth decided which varna a person belonged to.  This setup shaped daily life for years afterward.

Years into this faith, a prince named Siddhartha Gautama gave up his easy life.  He had seen how much plain suffering filled the world.  He taught that suffering grows from craving, wanting things to be other than they are.  He taught that a strict path could end that craving for good.  His followers called him the Buddha, meaning the awakened one.  His teaching grew into a path open to anyone, no matter which varna a person had been born into.

Years later, an emperor named Ashoka ruled the Maurya Empire.  By then, it was the biggest state the Indian subcontinent had ever seen.  Early in his reign, Ashoka waged a brutal war against the kingdom of Kalinga.  His own carved words tell of a huge number of dead and captured.  They tell of his own horror at what the war had cost.  After Kalinga, Ashoka took up Buddhist ways.  He turned his huge state toward a strikingly new goal.  He had edicts cut into pillars and rock faces across his empire, pushing nonviolence, tolerance of other faiths, and the good of plain people, not more war.

Few rulers in the old record changed course that plainly.  Fewer still left the proof cut in stone for a Recorder to find, more than two thousand years later.

passages.title: Case File: Two Schools of Thought, One Unifying Emperor
passages.text:
The Huang He, known in English as the Yellow River, flooded often and hard.  Later writers gave it the name China's Sorrow.  Its floodwaters also carried rich soil that made the river valley worth the risk.  Early Chinese life grew up right along its banks.

China's earliest well-known dynasty was the Shang, which gave way to the Zhou dynasty.  The Zhou brought in an idea called the Mandate of Heaven.  Heaven gave a ruler the right to rule only while that ruler ruled fairly.  Heaven could pull that right back from a ruler who did not.  Zhou power weakened over the years.  China broke apart into rival states that fought nearly nonstop, in a time later called the Warring States era.

Two very different schools of thought tried to answer that long disorder.  Confucius taught that harmony grows from everyone filling their role well.  A ruler should act fairly, a child should honor a parent, and a friend should treat a friend with respect.  Order, in his teaching, comes from virtue lived by everyone at once.  A different path is tied to a teacher known as Laozi.  His teaching pointed closer to the other side.  It held that people should follow the Dao, the natural way of the world, without forcing events against their own natural course.

Neither school ended the fighting.  A ruler named Ying Zheng did.  He beat every rival state and named himself Qin Shi Huangdi, China's first emperor.  He set one standard for the empire's writing, money, and weights.  One system replaced the many different ones lands had used before.  He also moved right against ideas that threatened his new power.  Records written later say he ordered rival texts burned, with Confucian works a main target.  A number of scholars who defied the order were put to death too.  This is the record this file's own title borrows its warning from.

passages.title: Case File: The Han Restoration and the Long Road West
passages.text:
The Qin dynasty fell apart only a few years after its first emperor died.  Harsh rule and open revolt wore it down fast.  The Han dynasty that came next ruled far longer.  It made a choice the Qin never had.  Han rulers stopped treating Confucian teaching as a threat and put it back at the very center of government instead.

Han officials had to study the Confucian classics, the same texts the Qin had once tried to burn.  A person's grasp of those texts more and more shaped who could serve the state.  That change built a government of trained scholar-officials.  Birth alone no longer decided who ran the country, a lasting shift in how China chose its leaders.

Han China also reached much farther than its own borders.  A long web of trade routes linked Han cities to Central Asia and beyond.  Later writers called this web the Silk Road.  Caravans carried Chinese silk west and brought back horses, glass, and goods from far regions in return.  A Han official named Zhang Qian is often credited with opening these links.  He traveled west on a state trip, though trade along parts of the route likely came before his trip.  Goods were never the only thing moving along that road.  Ideas and faiths traveled with the traders who carried them.

Buddhism reached China this way, coming slowly from India along the same routes the silk traders used.  Buddhism took root beside Confucianism and Daoism rather than replacing either one.  Chinese thought, from that point on, kept following the very same road.

passages.title: Case File: Closing the File on Rome
passages.text:
This is the last entry in the whole case file.  It closes in a different way than every entry before it.  Rome does not open a new puzzle.  It answers back into every puzzle this file has already opened.

Rome began as a kingdom, then threw out its own king and became a republic instead.  Two elected consuls led it, along with a council called the Senate.  For years afterward, rich patrician families held nearly all the real power.  Plain plebeian citizens fought for a bigger share of it.  That fight in time produced the Twelve Tables, Rome's first written law code.  The code was posted in public so that every citizen, patrician or plebeian, could actually see the same laws applied to all, even though rank still shaped much of Roman life.  Compare that to Hammurabi's own code, filed at the very start of this record.  Its finished laws still punished the same crime in different ways, depending on who the victim was.

Rome's spot on a sea-facing peninsula pushed it steadily outward.  Rome fought the rival city of Carthage across three long wars and won.  Rome then held most of the Mediterranean coast.  A road web linked it all, moving troops and officials fast across huge distances.

The republic itself could not survive its own success.  A general named Julius Caesar seized power by force.  Senators feared he wished to rule as a king, and they killed him.  More years of civil war came next.  His adopted heir, Octavian, rose as Rome's first emperor, taking the name Augustus.  A republic without a king had lasted nearly five hundred years before an empire took its place.

Rome gave out citizenship widely across its conquered lands, a reach that went far past Athens and its own narrow assembly.  Athens had let its citizens vote right on the city's own laws, years earlier.  Rome also matched many of its own gods to Greek ones, treating each pair as one god under two names.  Rome took in Greek philosophy too.  The file that opened with a river and a code of law now closes with an empire, one built from nearly every civilization this record has ever checked.

passages.title: Recovered Entry: What the Clay Kept
passages.text:
This entry answers a question every new Recorder asks.  Why does so much of the oldest record come from one flat, muddy plain?  The answer is clay.  Southern Mesopotamia had almost no stone and very little timber, but it had river mud without limit.  Scribes there wrote on wet clay tablets, and clay is stubborn.  A tablet dropped in a ruin simply waits.

The first cities on that plain were Sumerian.  Uruk and Ur each ran its own government, guarded its own walls, and honored its own patron god.  A stepped temple platform called a ziggurat stood at the center of many of them.  Villages had grown into cities, and cities needed records.  The earliest tablets are not poems or laws at all.  They are receipts, counting sacks of grain, jars of oil, and heads of livestock.  Others are school exercises, copied out by students learning the script, with the mistakes still sitting on them.

The tablets also show who stood where.  Kings and priests sat at the top, and merchants, artisans, and farmers came next.  Enslaved people sat at the bottom, many of them captives taken in war.

Those same centuries produced tools the whole world later borrowed.  Potters shaped clay on a turning wheel, and heavy carts rolled on wheels too.  Farmers cut furrows with a plow instead of a digging stick, and sailors caught the wind with a sail.  Metalworkers mixed copper with tin to make bronze, which held an edge far better than either metal alone.

No city on that plain stayed free forever.  A ruler named Sargon conquered the Sumerian cities and ruled them from Akkad, his own capital, and many historians call what he built the first empire in the record.  Babylon rose later, under the king whose law code this file already holds, and Assyria rose to dominate the region later still.

Here is the part the Office likes best.  Fire destroys most records, but fire bakes clay harder.  Palaces on that plain burned more than once, and the tablets stored inside came out of the ashes tougher than they went in.  The record survives partly because somebody's city was sacked.

passages.title: Case File: The Kingdom That Split in Two
passages.text:
The Office keeps one rule for sacred texts.  Read them for what they claim.  Then look for anything outside them that touches the same claim.  This entry is the best case in the archive for that rule.

The Hebrew Bible describes Solomon's kingdom breaking apart soon after he died, around nine hundred thirty BCE.  The northern tribes pulled away and formed a kingdom called Israel.  The northern kingdom's capital came to be a city named Samaria.  In that account, the southern tribes kept the line of David and the Temple in Jerusalem, in a smaller kingdom called Judah.  In that account, two kingdoms now stood where one had stood before.

Then the outside evidence arrives, and it is unusually good.  A carved stone known as the Mesha Stele was raised by a king of Moab.  It names Omri, a king of Israel, as an enemy who had pressed hard on Moab.  An Assyrian monument known as the Black Obelisk lists tribute paid to an Assyrian king.  It names Jehu, a later king of Israel, among those who paid.  Neither stone was cut to prove the Hebrew Bible right.  Each was cut to praise its own king, which is exactly why the Office weighs it.

The northern kingdom fell to Assyria.  Assyrian armies took Samaria around seven hundred twenty-two BCE, and Assyrian royal records report the capture in their own words.  Those records do not fully agree about which king finished the siege, and the Office files that disagreement rather than smoothing it away.  Assyria then moved many of the defeated people to other parts of its empire.  Newcomers were settled in their place.

The account preserved in the Hebrew Bible explains the fall in its own terms.  It describes the defeat as a punishment for abandoning the covenant.  That reasoning belongs to the account, and the Office records it as the account's own.

Much later, stories grew up about ten lost tribes still wandering somewhere.  The Office files those stories as legend.  Judah lasted longer than its northern neighbor did.  What finally happened to Judah is filed under the exile that followed.

passages.title: Case File: The Gods of the Everyday
passages.text:
This file is often misread, so the Office states its limits first.  There was no single Greek religion with one book and one creed.  Many Greek cities honored the same gods under the same names.  What each city actually did about it varied from place to place.

Every city had a god it counted as its own.  Athens honored Athena, and her festival, the Panathenaia, filled the city's streets.  A long procession climbed to the temples above the city and carried a newly woven robe for the goddess's statue.  Another Athenian festival honored Dionysus with days of plays, performed in the open air before large crowds.  Greek drama begins inside a religious festival, not beside one.

The games at Olympia worked the same way.  Athletes competed there in honor of Zeus, on ground that held his temple.  A truce was announced so that competitors and spectators could travel safely.  Modern readers file the Olympics under sport.  The people who founded them filed them under worship.

Cities also kept calendars of offerings, listing which animal was owed to which god on which day.  Some of those calendars were carved into stone, and pieces of them survive.  That is the Office's favorite kind of evidence: a working document nobody wrote for posterity.

Practice reached inside the house too.  Many households kept a hearth fire in the home and made small offerings there.  Stone pillars topped with a carved head stood at doorways and street corners in Athens, and people passing by honored them in small ways.

The most famous oracle of all was Delphi, a shrine to Apollo.  A priestess there, called the Pythia, answered questions put to her by whole cities and by ordinary people.  Worshippers believed she spoke for the god.  Her answers were often hard to read, and more than one city read one the way it already wanted to.  The Office records what people did at Delphi, and what they believed while they did it.  It files no verdict on the rest.

passages.title: Case File: One Witness, One Long War
passages.text:
The Office files this war under a warning label.  Much of what is known about it traces back to one man.  His part in the story comes at the end of this entry, where a Recorder can weigh it properly.

Athens and Sparta fought for twenty-seven years, from four hundred thirty-one to four hundred four BCE.  Each led a group of allied cities.  Athens had the stronger navy and an empire of tribute-paying allies.  Sparta had the stronger army.  Neither could easily reach the other's strength, which is one reason the war ran so long.

A sickness struck crowded, walled-in Athens beginning in four hundred thirty BCE, and it returned more than once over the next few years.  It killed the Athenian leader Pericles in four hundred twenty-nine BCE.  Ancient writers described the symptoms in detail.  Modern scholars still argue about what the disease actually was, so the Office files it as unidentified.

A truce called the Peace of Nicias, signed in four hundred twenty-one BCE, was supposed to end the fighting.  It held poorly and broke down.  Athens then sent a large fleet and army against the city of Syracuse, on the island of Sicily, between four hundred fifteen and four hundred thirteen BCE.  Almost none of that force came home.

Persia then paid for a Spartan fleet, and Spartan ships became a match for Athenian ones at last.  At Aegospotami in four hundred five BCE, Sparta destroyed the Athenian navy in a single action.  Athens surrendered the next year.  Its long defensive walls were pulled down, and a group of thirty men was installed to rule the city.

Sparta's turn on top did not last.  A Theban army beat a Spartan one at Leuctra in three hundred seventy-one BCE, and Spartan dominance ended there.

Now the warning label.  The fullest account of this war was written by an Athenian general who served in it, lost a command, and spent his exile writing.  He is a first-rate witness with a stake in the story.  His account also stops years before the war ends, so the last stretch comes from other writers.  The Office files the war as record and the telling as evidence with an interest attached.

passages.title: Case File: A Visitor's Notes and a Number That Traveled
passages.text:
Two pieces of evidence anchor this entry.  One is a traveler's notebook.  The other is a number.

Rulers of the Gupta family united much of northern India starting around three hundred twenty CE.  Later writers often call the centuries that followed a golden age.  The Office prefers a plainer description.  Courts paid for scholars, and the work those scholars did still turns up in daily life around the world.

A scholar named Aryabhata, born in four hundred seventy-six CE, wrote a short book on astronomy and mathematics.  He worked out a value for the ratio between a circle's rim and the line straight across it, close enough to stay useful for centuries.  He also argued that the earth turns on its own axis, which is why the stars appear to move across the sky.  Other scholars in the same tradition wrote on medicine and on the paths of the planets.

The number system matters more than any single scholar.  Indian mathematicians wrote with ten symbols and gave each one a value based on where it sat.  A symbol for zero held the empty place.  Arabic-speaking scholars took up the system and carried it west.  Europe learned it from them and called the symbols Arabic numerals, which is why much of the world still calls them that.  The name credits the messenger and skips the sender.  The Office files the correction and moves on.

Now the notebook.  A Chinese Buddhist monk named Faxian walked overland to India around four hundred CE, stayed for years, and wrote down what he saw.  He was not writing to flatter an Indian king, because he did not serve one.  He came for Buddhist texts and described everything else along the way.  An outside witness with no stake in a ruler's reputation is rare in this record, and the Office weighs him accordingly.

Two long poems, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, were also being copied and recited through these centuries.  Tradition names an author for each.  Both poems grew over so many centuries that the Office files those names as tradition rather than as record.

passages.title: Recovered Entry: The Third School, and the Paper That Followed
passages.text:
The Office's earlier entry on China sets two schools of thought side by side.  Neither of them is the one the Qin state actually ran on.  This entry files the third.

The school the Qin ran on is called Legalism.  It taught that people behave well only when rules are clear, rewards are certain, and punishments are heavy.  Virtue, in its view, was too slow and too rare to hold a state together.  It held that law should fall on everyone the same way, whatever a person's rank.  A thinker named Han Fei set the argument out most fully.  Qin had run on these ideas long before him.  A minister named Shang Yang rebuilt the state around them, generations before the first emperor.  Another minister, Li Si, later carried them into the unified empire.  The Qin's harsh reputation follows from those choices.  What the Qin then did to rival texts is already filed, on the strength of records written later.

The Han dynasty that came next put Confucian teaching at the center.  Legalist habits did not leave with the Qin, though.  Han law kept much of the same machinery, and later dynasties kept it too.

Han workshops also solved a problem the Office cares about more than most.  Before paper, Chinese writers used strips of bamboo tied into bundles, which were heavy.  They also used silk, which was costly.  A court official named Cai Lun was credited in one hundred five CE with a better method, using bark, rag, and worn-out fishing net beaten into pulp.  Scraps of older paper have turned up since, so the craft was already in use before he improved it.  Cheap writing material changes what gets written down and what gets copied.  Everything after this point in the Chinese record is thicker because of it.

Other Han work survives in the same practical spirit.  Han histories credit an official named Zhang Heng with an instrument built in one hundred thirty-two CE.  Those histories say it registered a distant earth tremor and showed which direction it came from.  Han doctors wrote medical texts that were still being studied centuries later.

The dynasty itself came apart around two hundred twenty CE, worn down by revolts, court struggles, and generals who stopped listening.  China broke into rival states again.

passages.title: Recovered Entry: The Earliest Letters in the File
passages.text:
The Office files this entry under its strictest rule.  A Recorder records what people believed, never a belief as a fact.

Rome ruled the province of Judea through officials it sent.  The record holds that a teacher named Jesus, from Galilee, was put to death there.  The method was crucifixion, a Roman way of killing.  The governor was a Roman named Pontius Pilate.  The year was near thirty CE.  A Roman writer named Tacitus reports the same death under that governor.  He wrote generations later, from outside the movement.  That is why the Office files the death as record.

His followers taught that he was the Messiah, a deliverer they found promised in their scriptures.  They came to believe he rose from the dead after the execution.  They believed his life carried those promises out.  The Office cannot check that.  What it files is that people held these beliefs, and held them early.

The earliest Christian writings in the record are letters, not stories about Jesus.  A man named Paul wrote them in the fifties CE.  They went mostly to small groups in cities around the eastern Mediterranean.  Scholars accept seven of them as surely his own.  A later book called Acts describes Paul traveling from city to city.  Acts and Paul's own letters do not always agree on where he went, or when.  So the Office files those routes as described, never as settled.

Roman officials moved against the movement at times, but not steadily, and rarely everywhere.  Nero punished believers in the city of Rome after a fire there, in sixty-four CE.  Decius ordered everyone in the empire to offer sacrifice to the Roman gods in two hundred fifty CE.  No earlier order like it had reached the whole empire.  A longer stretch of pressure ran from three hundred three to three hundred eleven CE.

In three hundred thirteen CE, Constantine and a fellow emperor granted freedom of worship to every religion, not to one.  That order did not make Christianity the empire's religion, whatever later accounts say.  Theodosius did that in three hundred eighty CE.

The movement spread along Rome's roads and sea lanes.  A shared Greek language helped.  So did communities already living in cities across the empire.  Growth was steady rather than sudden.  Maybe one person in ten in the empire had joined by three hundred CE, maybe far fewer.  The Office has filed one arc like this before.  The entries on Buddhism's spread followed trade routes and an emperor's backing.  The Office ranks neither.

passages.title: Case File Addendum: The Long Ending
passages.text:
The closing entry on Rome is filed and sealed.  This addendum sits behind it for one reason.  The file closed on an empire that had not finished happening yet.

The two centuries after Augustus ran quieter inside the borders than the years before them had.  Later writers gave that stretch its name, the Pax Romana, the Roman peace.  Goods moved along paved roads and safe sea lanes.  Roman coins worked across a huge stretch of ground.  Engineers built aqueducts that carried water for miles, and they used concrete to raise vaults and domes that still stand today.

The quiet did not hold, and in the two hundreds CE the empire nearly came apart.  Armies made and unmade emperors at speed.  Borders came under pressure from groups pushing in from outside.  Coins carried less and less silver, and prices climbed.

Later emperors held the thing together by changing its shape, and Diocletian split the work of ruling among several men.  Constantine moved the capital east, to a Greek city he rebuilt and renamed for himself.  In three hundred ninety-five CE the empire was divided into a western half and an eastern half, each with its own ruler.

The western half thinned out over the next hundred years.  Rome itself was sacked, in four hundred ten and again in four hundred fifty-five CE.  In four hundred seventy-six CE a commander removed the last emperor the west still had, and put no one in his place.

The eastern half did not fall then.  Ruled from Constantinople, it lasted nearly another thousand years.  Its own people called themselves Romans, in Greek, and rarely used any other name for their state.  Much later, European scholars began calling that empire Byzantine, a name its own people never used for their empire.

That is this record's closing warning, and it fits every file in the drawer.  A phrase like the fall of Rome sounds like a single event.  What the evidence shows is a government ending in one half, a government carrying on in the other, and roads, law, and language living on past both.  Names get applied by whoever writes last, and checking who applied a name, and when, is the whole job.

partA.stem: According to the briefing, why did Egypt unite into a civilization sooner than the pattern in Mesopotamia?
choices: The Nile flooded on a far steadier yearly schedule, and deserts on both sides kept most invaders away.
The Tigris and the Euphrates flooded every year, spreading fresh soil across the land nearby.
Managing floodwater in Mesopotamia took real teamwork, canals, walls, and shared rules.
Farming grew more food than hunting ever had, so people could settle down.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The floods were hard to predict, though, coming early some years and late in others.
Farming grew more food than hunting ever had, and extra food let some people stop searching for their next meal.
Deserts on both sides of the Nile kept most invaders away, and a steadier, safer valley let Egypt unite sooner.
Managing that water took real teamwork, canals, walls, and shared rules.

distractorRationale.1: This is true of Mesopotamia's rivers, but the passage credits Egypt's unity to the Nile's steadier schedule and the deserts, not to Mesopotamia's flooding.
distractorRationale.2: This describes the extra teamwork Mesopotamia's unpredictable floods required, the opposite of why Egypt needed less of that kind of organizing.
distractorRationale.3: This explains why farming let people settle down at all, a step every river-valley civilization shared, not the specific reason Egypt united sooner than Mesopotamia.

items.explain: The passage states directly that a steadier river and safer valley, thanks to protective deserts, let Egypt unite sooner than the flood-prone, harder-to-predict pattern in Mesopotamia.  The other choices each describe a true detail about rivers or farming that does not answer why Egypt specifically united faster.

items.stem: According to the case file, what does ma'at mean to Egyptians?
choices: The balance across the whole world that Egyptians believed the pharaoh's divine power was meant to keep.
The written record Mesopotamian scribes pressed into wet clay using a cut reed.
The peace deal Ramses the Second signed after reigning for decades.
The name of the trading trip Hatshepsut sent south along the coast.

distractorRationale.1: That describes cuneiform, Mesopotamia's writing system, a completely different topic from ma'at, the balance Egyptians believed their pharaoh's power was meant to keep.
distractorRationale.2: That peace deal is a specific achievement credited to Ramses the Second, not the word ma'at, which names a broader belief about balance tied to kingship itself.
distractorRationale.3: Hatshepsut's trading trip is a specific achievement of her own reign, not the word ma'at, which names the world-balance Egyptians believed every pharaoh's power was meant to keep.

items.explain: The case file states directly that Egyptians believed their pharaoh's main job was keeping the whole world in balance, a balance they called ma'at, tied to his divine power.  Each wrong choice names a real but separate detail, a writing system or a specific ruler's achievement, rather than the balance the word ma'at itself names.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state the code's own opening promise of fair, equal protection.
spans: A careless builder whose work kills a house owner is put to death.
Its laws exist so that a strong man cannot crush a weak one.
They exist so that a widow or an orphan can get a fair hearing.
The punishment changes with the victim's standing.
If the victim holds the same high standing, the attacker's own eye is destroyed in return.
items.explain: The code's opening lines promise fair treatment for everyone, protecting a weak man from a strong one and giving a widow or an orphan a fair hearing.  The other three sentences describe what the actual clauses do once a real case is decided, which is exactly the gap this entry is filed to weigh.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the case file on Egypt and Kush.
choices: Egyptians believed the pharaoh held a kind of divine power.
Mesopotamian scribes carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone.
Egypt's own armies took over Kush during Egypt's strongest era.
Egypt and Kush never traded goods with each other.
Kushite kings later conquered Egypt and ruled it as pharaohs.

distractorRationale.1: The passage says Egyptian scribes carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone, while Mesopotamian scribes pressed cuneiform into wet clay instead; this choice swaps which people used which system.
distractorRationale.3: The passage says Egypt and Kush traded gold, ivory, and other goods for centuries; it never says they had no trade at all.

items.explain: All three correct details come straight from the case file: the pharaoh's believed divine power, Egypt's early control over Kush, and Kush's later conquest of Egypt.  The two wrong choices each invert a real detail, swapping which civilization used which writing system or denying a trade relationship the passage actually describes.

partA.stem: What is the real dispute the Provenance Office files about Hammurabi's Code?
choices: Whether the code's opening promise of fairness actually matches what its clauses did for people of different social standing.
Whether the stone the code was carved on is a forgery.
Whether Hammurabi actually ruled Babylon in ancient Mesopotamia.
Whether the code covered house builders as well as merchants and farmers.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Hammurabi was a king of Babylon in ancient Mesopotamia.
The dispute is what the code actually did for the people living under it.
Other surviving clauses cover house builders, merchants, and farmers.
The stone the code was carved on still exists.

distractorRationale.1: The passage explicitly says the dispute is not whether the code is real, so a forgery question is not the actual dispute this file weighs.
distractorRationale.2: The passage confirms Hammurabi ruled Babylon as simple background, not as a contested claim; nothing in the entry treats this as disputed.
distractorRationale.3: The passage lists house builders as one group covered by surviving clauses, but this is a factual detail, not the dispute the office is weighing.

items.explain: The entry states directly that the dispute is not whether the code is real, but what the code actually did for the people living under it, meaning whether its opening promise of fairness matches its actual, unequal clauses.  The other choices each restate a background fact from the passage rather than naming the real, unresolved dispute.

items.stem: Match each river system or region to what the case file says actually happened there.
rowLabels: The Tigris and the Euphrates in Mesopotamia
The kingdom of Kush, south of Egypt along the same river
colLabels: Flooded on a far steadier yearly schedule, and protective deserts on both sides let Egypt unite sooner
Traded gold and ivory with Egypt for centuries, and its own kings later conquered Egypt and ruled it as pharaohs
Flooded every year, but unpredictably, so managing the water took real teamwork: canals, walls, and shared rules
items.explain: The case file credits each region with its own specific role: Mesopotamia's two unpredictable rivers demanded real teamwork to manage, Egypt's steadier Nile and protective deserts let it unite sooner, and Kush traded with Egypt for centuries before its own kings eventually conquered Egypt and ruled it themselves.  Swapping which region caused which outcome is exactly the confusion this table is built to catch.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly describes something the case file credits to Hatshepsut?
choices: She reigned for decades and later signed one of the oldest peace deals in the whole record.
She ruled Egypt in her own right as a full pharaoh, not merely as a king's wife, and sent a famous trading trip south along the coast.
She conquered Egypt from the south and ruled it as pharaoh while keeping many Egyptian customs of her own.
She pressed wedge-shaped cuneiform marks into wet clay to record her own achievements.

distractorRationale.0: The case file credits that long reign and peace deal to Ramses the Second, a different pharaoh from Hatshepsut.
distractorRationale.2: That conquest belongs to Kush's kings, who later conquered Egypt itself; the case file never says Hatshepsut conquered Egypt from outside it.
distractorRationale.3: Cuneiform is the writing system the case file credits to Mesopotamian scribes; Egyptian scribes, including any recording of Hatshepsut's reign, used hieroglyphs instead.

items.explain: The case file credits Hatshepsut directly with ruling Egypt in her own right as a full pharaoh and sending a famous trading trip south along the coast, a different achievement from Ramses's long reign and peace deal.  Each wrong choice borrows an achievement, event, or writing system that the case file credits to a different ruler or civilization entirely.

items.stem: Egyptian scribes instead drew or carved {{0}} onto papyrus and stone, a system built from hundreds of small pictures.

choices: hieroglyphs
cuneiform
ma'at

distractorRationale.1: Cuneiform is the wedge-shaped writing system Mesopotamian scribes pressed into wet clay with a cut reed, not the picture-based system Egyptian scribes carved onto papyrus and stone.
distractorRationale.2: Ma'at names the balance the pharaoh was believed to keep in the world, not a writing system at all.

items.quote: Egyptian scribes instead drew or carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone, a system built from hundreds of small pictures.
items.explain: The case file credits Egyptian scribes with hieroglyphs, a picture-based system carved onto papyrus and stone, while Mesopotamian scribes used the separate wedge-shaped cuneiform system instead.  Ma'at names a belief about balance, not either civilization's writing system, so it cannot fill this blank.

partA.stem: According to the recovered entry, what actually happened when a man destroyed the eye of a person of common standing?
choices: The attacker paid a sum of silver instead of losing his own eye in return.
The attacker's own eye was destroyed in return, exactly as for a victim of high standing.
The attacker paid half the payment required for harming an enslaved person.
The attacker was put to death, the same punishment used for a careless builder.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: If the victim holds the same high standing, the attacker's own eye is destroyed in return.
It sets the payment lower still, at half the enslaved person's own value, paid to that person's owner.
It orders a payment of silver instead of a matching injury.
A careless builder whose work kills a house owner is put to death.

distractorRationale.1: That punishment, an eye for an eye, is what the clause sets for a victim of high standing, not common standing, according to the very next sentence in the entry.
distractorRationale.2: That sentence describes the payment set for an injury done to an enslaved person, half that person's own value paid to the owner, a different price entirely from the silver payment set for a victim of common standing.
distractorRationale.3: Death is the punishment the entry gives for a careless builder whose work kills a house owner, a completely different clause about builders, not the eye-injury clause.

items.explain: The entry states plainly that the clause covering an injury to a man of common standing orders a payment of silver instead of a matching injury, a lighter punishment than the eye-for-eye penalty set for a victim of high standing.  Each wrong choice borrows the real punishment set for a different rank or a different clause entirely.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that show which side held power over the other actually changed over time between Egypt and Kush.
spans: Egypt and Kush traded gold, ivory, and other goods for centuries, but their bond was never simply friendly.
South of Egypt, along the same river, sat the kingdom of Kush.
Egypt's own armies took over Kush during Egypt's strongest era.
Kushite kings conquered Egypt itself and ruled it as pharaohs in their own right, keeping many Egyptian customs alongside their own.
Both systems did the same basic job.
items.explain: The case file traces a real reversal: Egypt's own armies once controlled Kush, but years later Kushite kings conquered Egypt and ruled it themselves as pharaohs.  The other three sentences give true background about location, trade, or writing, none of which shows which side actually held power over the other.

partA.stem: According to the case file, why did Egyptians develop mummification and build elaborate tombs?
choices: They believed a spirit needed a preserved body to survive into the next life.
They believed the pharaoh alone needed a preserved body to keep the world in balance.
They wanted a written record of each person's achievements to survive.
They believed Kush would conquer Egypt and wanted to protect their belongings.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: His main job was keeping the whole world in balance, a balance Egyptians called ma'at.
Kushite kings conquered Egypt itself and ruled it as pharaohs in their own right, keeping many Egyptian customs alongside their own.
Egyptians believed a spirit needed a preserved body to survive into the next life, so skilled workers made mummies to stop a body from decaying.
The two peoples even wrote their history in different ways.

distractorRationale.1: That sentence describes the pharaoh's duty to keep ma'at in balance, a different belief about kingship, not the funerary belief behind mummies and tombs, which the passage says applied to preserving a person's spirit generally.
distractorRationale.2: That sentence is about how the two civilizations recorded their history in writing, cuneiform versus hieroglyphs, not about why bodies were preserved after death.
distractorRationale.3: That sentence describes Kush's later conquest of Egypt, a political event with no connection to the belief that drove mummification.

items.explain: The passage states directly that Egyptians believed a spirit needed a preserved body to survive into the next life, which is why skilled workers made mummies and wealthy families built tombs stocked with needed goods.  The other choices each point to a true but unrelated detail from elsewhere in the passage.

items.stem: According to the case file, how did Mesopotamian scribes' writing method differ from Egyptian scribes'?
choices: Mesopotamian scribes carved hieroglyphs into stone, while Egyptian scribes pressed cuneiform into wet clay.
Both sets of scribes used the exact same wedge-shaped cuneiform system, just carved into different materials.
Mesopotamian scribes pressed wedge-shaped cuneiform marks into wet clay with a cut reed, while Egyptian scribes drew or carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone.
Egyptian scribes left behind no written record at all, unlike Mesopotamian scribes.

distractorRationale.0: This reverses which civilization used which system; the case file credits cuneiform to Mesopotamian scribes and hieroglyphs to Egyptian scribes, not the other way around.
distractorRationale.1: The case file describes two different systems, wedge-shaped cuneiform pressed into clay and picture-based hieroglyphs carved onto papyrus and stone, not one shared system.
distractorRationale.3: The case file says Egyptian scribes did leave a written record, hieroglyphs carved onto papyrus and stone; it is the separate Indus civilization, in a later file, whose script survives unread.

items.explain: The case file describes two distinct systems: Mesopotamian scribes pressed wedge-shaped cuneiform marks into wet clay with a cut reed, one tablet at a time, while Egyptian scribes instead drew or carved hieroglyphs onto papyrus and stone.  The other choices each reverse which civilization used which system, deny that two systems existed, or borrow the wrong civilization's own writing gap.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what was Abraham's covenant an exchange for, according to the Hebrew Bible?
choices: A promise of land and heirs, in exchange for loyalty to one God alone.
Freedom from slavery in Egypt, in exchange for following a new code of law.
A Temple built in Jerusalem, in exchange for uniting the tribes.
Protection during the family's years in Egypt, in exchange for guarding sacred texts.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: It tells of Moses leading them out of that slavery.
David's son Solomon built the First Temple there, one central place for the tradition's most sacred rites.
In exchange, that account describes a covenant, a solemn promise of land and heirs.
It describes Abraham as the first to promise loyalty to one God alone.

distractorRationale.1: Moses leading the people out of slavery is the Exodus, a later event, not what Abraham's own covenant was exchanged for.
distractorRationale.2: Solomon's Temple came generations after Abraham and is not part of Abraham's own covenant exchange.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence names Abraham's promise of loyalty itself, the giving side of the exchange, not what he received in return for it.

items.explain: The passage states directly that Abraham's covenant was an exchange: he promised loyalty to one God alone, and in exchange, that account describes a promise of land and heirs.  The other choices each point to a true detail from later in the tradition's history, not to what the covenant itself exchanged.

items.stem: According to the case file, what did Solomon do as Israel's third king?
choices: He united the tribes more firmly and made Jerusalem his capital for the first time.
He led the people out of slavery in Egypt, an event remembered as the Exodus.
He became Israel's very first king, after years of being led only by judges.
He built the First Temple in Jerusalem, one central place for the tradition's most sacred rites.

distractorRationale.0: The case file credits that union and choice of capital to David, Solomon's father, not to Solomon himself.
distractorRationale.1: That event is credited to Moses, generations before any king ruled Israel; Solomon reigned long after the Exodus.
distractorRationale.2: Saul, not Solomon, is named as the first king; Solomon was David's son and Israel's third king.

items.explain: The case file states plainly that David's son Solomon built the First Temple in Jerusalem, becoming one central place for the tradition's most sacred rites.  Each wrong choice borrows an achievement, uniting the tribes, leading the Exodus, or becoming the first king, that the case file credits to a different figure earlier in the same story.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that introduce the Israelites' move toward loyalty to one God alone as something new.
spans: Most peoples in the old Near East worshipped many gods at once.
The Hebrew Bible describes something different taking root among a group later known as the Israelites.
It describes Abraham as the first to promise loyalty to one God alone.
In exchange, that account describes a covenant, a solemn promise of land and heirs.
This whole file keeps coming back to that belief.
items.explain: The file introduces the new belief directly: something different took root among the Israelites, and Abraham is named as the first to promise loyalty to one God alone.  The other sentences describe the surrounding peoples' many gods, the covenant's own terms, or a later note, none of which introduces the new belief itself.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the case file on how the tradition survived.
choices: The tradition rebuilt the Temple a third time to survive.
The Babylonian army destroyed the First Temple and forced many Israelites into exile.
A Roman army later destroyed the Second Temple during a revolt.
The diaspora describes Israelites returning to a single unified kingdom.
Yohanan ben Zakkai escaped the besieged city and opened a school at Yavneh.

distractorRationale.0: The passage says the tradition survived by not rebuilding its state or Temple, proving it had never truly depended on either one alone.
distractorRationale.3: The diaspora is the scattering of a people far from their own homeland, the opposite of returning to one unified kingdom.

items.explain: The three correct details trace the file's own sequence: the Babylonian destruction and exile, the Second Temple's later Roman destruction, and Yohanan ben Zakkai's school at Yavneh.  The two wrong choices each invert what the passage actually says about rebuilding and about what the diaspora means.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what changed when the Israelites moved from judges to kings?
choices: Saul became the first king, and David then united the tribes more firmly and made Jerusalem his capital.
Judges were replaced by a Temple that centered all worship in Jerusalem.
Moses received a code of law that renewed the covenant for the first time.
The tribes split permanently and never united under one ruler again.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: David's son Solomon built the First Temple there, one central place for the tradition's most sacred rites.
David, the second, united the tribes more firmly and made Jerusalem his capital.
It renewed the same covenant Abraham had made years before.
Saul became the first.

distractorRationale.1: The Temple came later, built by Solomon, David's son; it did not replace judges, kings did.
distractorRationale.2: Moses and his code of law come from the earlier Exodus story, well before Saul and David's kingship began.
distractorRationale.3: The passage says the opposite: David united the tribes more firmly, not that they split apart permanently.

items.explain: The case file states plainly that after judges, the Israelites united behind kings instead, starting with Saul, and then David united the tribes more firmly and made Jerusalem his capital.  The other choices each move a detail from a different part of the story into the wrong place in the sequence.

items.stem: The case file traces the tradition's own early history across five stages.  Put these five stages in the order they actually happened.
tiles: The Babylonian army destroys the First Temple and forces many Israelites into exile
Abraham promises loyalty to one God alone, and receives a covenant of land and heirs
Yohanan ben Zakkai opens a school at Yavneh, shifting the tradition toward study, prayer, and law
Moses leads the people out of slavery in Egypt, an event remembered as the Exodus
Saul becomes the first king, and David later unites the tribes and makes Jerusalem his capital
items.explain: The case file lays out this sequence directly: Abraham's covenant comes first, then Moses leads the Exodus out of slavery, then Saul and David establish the kingship, then the Babylonian army destroys the First Temple and forces exile, and only after that does Yohanan ben Zakkai open his school at Yavneh.  Placing the Temple's destruction before the kingship it followed, or the school before the loss that caused it, is exactly the confusion this sequence is built to catch.

items.stem: According to the case file, what actually happened to the Second Temple?
choices: A Roman army destroyed it during a revolt long after Israel's old kings had reigned.
The Babylonian army destroyed it and forced many Israelites into exile.
Persian rulers destroyed it soon after allowing the exiles to return and rebuild it.
It still stands today, since the case file never records its destruction.

distractorRationale.1: The Babylonian army destroyed the First Temple; the Second Temple was built later, after Persian rulers let the exiles return, and it was Rome that destroyed it.
distractorRationale.2: Persian rulers let the exiles return and build the Second Temple; the case file credits its destruction to a Roman army, not to Persian rulers.
distractorRationale.3: The case file states directly that a Roman army destroyed the Second Temple during a revolt; it does not say the Temple still stands.

items.explain: The case file states directly that the Second Temple stood for centuries before a Roman army destroyed it too, during a revolt long after Israel's old kings had reigned.  Each wrong choice either credits the wrong destroyer, the Babylonians instead of Rome, or denies that the Second Temple's own destruction happened at all.

items.stem: That one choice is the seed of {{0}}, the belief in exactly one God.

choices: monotheism
polytheism
covenant

distractorRationale.1: Polytheism means believing in many gods at once, the opposite of the one-God belief the passage says took root among the Israelites.
distractorRationale.2: Covenant names the solemn promise of land and heirs Abraham made with God, not the belief in exactly one God itself.

items.quote: That one choice is the seed of monotheism, the belief in exactly one God.
items.explain: The case file names the new belief directly as monotheism, the belief in exactly one God, planted by Abraham's choice of loyalty.  Polytheism names the opposite belief, many gods at once, and covenant names the promise exchanged, so neither term fits the blank here.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what happened after the Babylonian army conquered the kingdom of Judah?
choices: The army destroyed the First Temple and forced many Israelites into exile, far from their own land.
Persian rulers immediately let the exiles return and rebuild the Temple that same year.
A Roman army destroyed the Temple during a revolt.
Yohanan ben Zakkai opened a small school at Yavneh.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Then a Roman army destroyed it too, during a revolt long after Israel's old kings had reigned.
He got permission from Roman rulers to open a small school in a town called Yavneh.
The army destroyed the First Temple in Jerusalem and forced many Israelites into exile, far from their own land.
Years later, Persian rulers let the exiles return and build a Second Temple on that same site.

distractorRationale.1: The passage says this return happened years later, not immediately, and it describes the Second Temple's building, a separate later event from the Babylonian conquest itself.
distractorRationale.2: This describes the Second Temple's destruction by Rome, centuries after the Babylonian conquest of the First Temple, a different event entirely.
distractorRationale.3: Yohanan ben Zakkai's school came after the Temple's second and final destruction by Rome, a much later turn in the story, not a direct result of the Babylonian conquest.

items.explain: The passage states directly that the Babylonian army's conquest led straight to the First Temple's destruction and the exile of many Israelites, the event remembered as the diaspora.  The other choices each describe a real event from later in the tradition's history, wrongly placed right after the Babylonian conquest.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that describe exactly what changed at the center of the tradition once the Temple was gone for good.
spans: Priests had once made offerings in one sacred building.
Now study, prayer, and law took that place, and any group could carry those things with it, anywhere.
The record credits a teacher named Yohanan ben Zakkai with the turn that followed.
This second loss should have finished the tradition for good.
That exile is remembered as the diaspora.
items.explain: These two sentences state the actual shift: priests once made offerings in one sacred building, and afterward study, prayer, and law took that place, things any group could carry anywhere.  The other sentences name the teacher behind the change, restate how serious the loss was, or define an earlier term, without stating the shift itself.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what did Yohanan ben Zakkai's school at Yavneh actually change?
choices: It shifted the tradition's center from Temple sacrifice toward study, prayer, and law any community could carry anywhere.
It convinced the Roman army to rebuild the destroyed Temple.
It reunited the kingdom of Judah under a single king again.
It ended the diaspora and brought every exile back to Jerusalem.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Priests had once made offerings in one sacred building.
Now study, prayer, and law took that place, and any group could carry those things with it, anywhere.

items.stem: According to the case file, what did the Mandate of Heaven actually mean for a Zhou ruler?
choices: Heaven gave a ruler the right to rule only while that ruler ruled fairly, and Heaven could pull that right back from one who did not.
It meant a ruler's family would keep power forever, no matter how that ruler governed.
It meant only a ruler who defeated every rival state could ever claim the throne.
It meant Confucian texts had to be studied before anyone could serve as an official.

distractorRationale.1: The case file says the opposite: Heaven could pull the right to rule back from a ruler who did not rule fairly, so power was never guaranteed forever.
distractorRationale.2: Defeating every rival state describes Qin Shi Huangdi's own later path to power, a separate event from the Zhou's own idea about a ruler's fair conduct.
distractorRationale.3: That practice belongs to the later Han dynasty's own choice about choosing officials, a separate idea from the Zhou's Mandate of Heaven, about a ruler's own right to rule.

items.explain: The case file defines the Mandate of Heaven directly: Heaven gave a ruler the right to rule only while that ruler ruled fairly, and Heaven could pull that right back from a ruler who did not.  Each wrong choice attaches a permanent guarantee, a conquest requirement, or a Han-era practice that the case file credits to a different ruler or a different dynasty.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that give direct evidence of how the Han government actually chose its officials.

Han officials had to study the Confucian classics, the same texts the Qin had once tried to burn.
A person's grasp of those texts more and more shaped who could serve the state.
A long web of trade routes linked Han cities to Central Asia and beyond.

items.explain: The file states directly that Han officials had to study the Confucian classics, and a person's grasp of those texts increasingly shaped who could actually serve the state.  The other sentences describe the Qin's fall, the Silk Road's reach, or Buddhism's arrival, none of which is evidence of how officials were actually chosen.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the case file on Qin unification.

The Warring States era was a time of steady peace across China.

distractorRationale.4: The passage says Qin Shi Huangdi set one standard for the empire's writing, replacing the many different systems lands had used before, not letting each keep its own.

items.explain: The three correct details trace the file's own sequence: the Zhou's Mandate of Heaven, Ying Zheng's conquest and new title, and the burning of rival texts under his rule.  The two wrong choices each invert what the passage says about the Warring States era and about Qin's standardized writing system.

He also moved right against ideas that threatened his new power.
A number of scholars who defied the order were put to death too.
Records written later say he ordered rival texts burned, with Confucian works a main target.

distractorRationale.2: The passage says one system replaced the many different ones lands had used before, describing unification, the opposite of dividing the empire back into rival states.
distractorRationale.3: Opening trade routes to Central Asia is a Han dynasty achievement described in the next case file, not something this passage credits to Qin Shi Huangdi.

items.explain: The passage states directly that after standardizing writing, money, and weights, Qin Shi Huangdi moved against ideas that threatened his power, ordering rival texts, especially Confucian writings, burned, with defiant scholars put to death.  The other choices each borrow an achievement or event that belongs to a different ruler or a different case file.

items.stem: Match each idea to the school of thought the case file credits it to.

People should follow the Dao, the natural way of the world

Order comes without forcing events against their own natural course

Swapping which teacher goes with which idea is exactly the confusion this table is built to catch.

items.stem: According to the case file, what actually caused the Warring States era?
choices: Qin Shi Huangdi ordered rival texts burned, which broke China apart into fighting states.
Zhou power weakened over the years, and China broke apart into rival states that fought nearly nonstop.
The Han dynasty's collapse left China without any government at all.
A weaker monsoon and shifting rivers made farming too difficult to sustain a single ruler.

distractorRationale.0: Qin Shi Huangdi's burning of rival texts came after he had already unified China as its first emperor, ending the Warring States era rather than causing it.
distractorRationale.2: The Han dynasty is a later dynasty that came after the Qin; its own fall is a separate, later event from the earlier Warring States era.
distractorRationale.3: Weaker monsoons and shifting rivers are the case file's evidence for the Indus civilization's decline, in a different tile's file, not the cause of China's own Warring States era.

items.explain: The case file states directly that Zhou power weakened over the years, and China broke apart into rival states that fought nearly nonstop, in the era later called the Warring States era.  Each wrong choice borrows a cause from a later ruler, a different dynasty, or even a different civilization's own file entirely.

items.stem: The Zhou brought in an idea called the {{0}}.

Silk Road
Warring States era

distractorRationale.2: The Warring States era names the period of nonstop fighting after Zhou power weakened, an era, not the idea itself that explained a ruler's right to rule.

items.quote: The Zhou brought in an idea called the Mandate of Heaven.
items.explain: The Zhou dynasty introduced the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that a ruler's right to rule depended on ruling fairly and could be withdrawn.  The Silk Road and the Warring States era are both real terms from this same file, but neither one names that specific idea about a ruler's own right to rule.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what deliberate choice did the Han dynasty make that the Qin never had?
choices: Han rulers stopped treating Confucian teaching as a threat and placed it back at the center of government.
Han rulers banned all study of the Confucian classics permanently.
Han rulers let birth alone decide who could serve the state.
Han rulers closed every trade route the Qin had opened.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Birth alone no longer decided who ran the country, a lasting shift in how China chose its leaders.
Han officials had to study the Confucian classics, the same texts the Qin had once tried to burn.
Han China also reached much farther than its own borders.
Han rulers stopped treating Confucian teaching as a threat and put it back at the very center of government instead.

distractorRationale.2: The passage says birth alone no longer decided who ran the country under the Han, a lasting shift away from birth-based rule, not toward it.
distractorRationale.3: The passage says Han China reached much farther than its own borders, describing the Silk Road's growth, the opposite of closing any trade routes.

items.explain: The passage states the Han's deliberate choice directly: rulers stopped treating Confucian teaching as a threat and placed it back at the center of government, building a government of trained scholar-officials rather than relying on birth alone.  The other choices each state the reverse of a specific claim the passage makes about the Han.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that give this file's own evidence of ideas being deliberately destroyed, not merely lost.

Neither school ended the fighting.
He set one standard for the empire's writing, money, and weights.
Records written later say he ordered rival texts burned, with Confucian works a main target.
