The other sentences describe the Huang He's flooding, Qin standardization, or the era's fighting, all true background that does not describe the record being deliberately destroyed.

partA.stem: According to the case file, how did Buddhism reach China?
choices: It arrived gradually from India, carried along the same trade routes silk traders used.
It began in China and then spread outward to India along the Silk Road.
It replaced both Confucianism and Daoism completely once it arrived.
It arrived suddenly with a Han army sent to conquer India.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Buddhism took root beside Confucianism and Daoism rather than replacing either one.
Buddhism reached China this way, coming slowly from India along the same routes the silk traders used.
A Han official named Zhang Qian is often credited with opening these links.
Ideas and faiths traveled with the traders who carried them.

distractorRationale.1: Zhang Qian is credited with opening the Silk Road's western links from China's side, but the passage says Buddhism traveled the opposite direction, from India into China, not the reverse.
distractorRationale.2: The passage says the opposite: Buddhism took root beside Confucianism and Daoism, not replacing either one.
distractorRationale.3: The passage credits traders, not an army, with carrying ideas and faiths along the Silk Road; no conquest of India is mentioned anywhere in this file.

items.explain: The passage states directly that Buddhism reached China gradually from India, carried along the very same routes the silk traders used, and that it took root beside Confucianism and Daoism rather than replacing either one.  The other choices each reverse the route's direction or invent a method of arrival the passage never describes.

items.stem: According to the case file, what did caravans actually carry along the Silk Road?
choices: They carried only Confucian texts west, to spread scholar-official training beyond China's own borders.
They carried rival texts west specifically to have them burned outside China's own borders.
They carried Chinese silk west and brought back horses, glass, and goods from far regions in return.
They carried Buddhist monks only, since no ordinary goods moved along the route.

distractorRationale.0: The case file names silk as the good caravans carried west, along with ideas and faiths traveling with the traders; it never limits the caravans' cargo to Confucian texts alone.
distractorRationale.1: Burning rival texts is credited to Qin Shi Huangdi, generations before the Han dynasty's own Silk Road trade described here, and it happened inside China, not along any trade route.
distractorRationale.3: The case file says Buddhism reached China gradually as an idea traveling with traders, alongside real goods like silk, horses, and glass, not that only monks moved along the route.

items.explain: The case file states plainly that caravans carried Chinese silk west and brought back horses, glass, and goods from far regions in return, with ideas and faiths like Buddhism traveling alongside those traders.  Each wrong choice narrows the caravans' cargo to something the case file credits to a different ruler, a different era, or ideas alone rather than real traded goods.

partA.stem: According to the case file, how did Rome's Twelve Tables compare to Hammurabi's code, filed at the start of this record?
choices: The Twelve Tables were posted in public for every citizen to read, even though rank still shaped much of Roman life, while Hammurabi's code punished the same crime differently by rank.
Both codes were kept secret from ordinary citizens, and only kings and priests were ever allowed to know what they actually said.
Hammurabi's code punished every rank of society equally, exactly as the Twelve Tables did, so neither code treated a victim's standing as relevant.
The Twelve Tables were Rome's first attempt at law of any kind, just as Hammurabi's code was Mesopotamia's first attempt at law of any kind.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That fight in time produced the Twelve Tables, Rome's first written law code.
For years afterward, rich patrician families held nearly all the real power.
The code was posted in public so that every citizen, patrician or plebeian, could actually see the same laws applied to all, even though rank still shaped much of Roman life.
Its finished laws still punished the same crime in different ways, depending on who the victim was.

distractorRationale.1: The passage says patrician families held nearly all the real power for years, which explains a power imbalance, but it never claims either code was kept secret from ordinary citizens; the Twelve Tables were posted publicly precisely so laws could be seen.
distractorRationale.2: The passage says the opposite about Hammurabi's code: its finished laws still punished the same crime differently depending on who the victim was, not equally for every rank.
distractorRationale.3: The Twelve Tables were Rome's first written law code, but this passage never claims Hammurabi's code was Mesopotamia's very first law of any kind, only that it is the record's earliest filed dispute.

items.explain: The passage draws the comparison directly: the Twelve Tables were posted in public for every citizen to read, even though rank still shaped much of Roman life, while Hammurabi's code, filed at the start of this record, punished the same crime differently depending on the victim's standing.  The other choices each state the reverse of a specific claim or add a detail the passage does not support.

items.stem: According to the closing file, what happened when Rome threw out its own king?
choices: It became an empire immediately, ruled by a single emperor from that point on.
It kept the same king in place, but stripped him of any real power.
It split permanently into two separate, independent city-states.
It became a republic instead, led by two elected consuls and a council called the Senate.

distractorRationale.0: The case file says Rome's shift to empire came centuries later, after Julius Caesar's rise and Augustus becoming Rome's first emperor, not right after the king was thrown out.
distractorRationale.1: The case file says Rome threw out its own king entirely and became a republic instead, not that it kept the king as a powerless figurehead.
distractorRationale.2: The case file describes Rome uniting under elected consuls and a Senate as one republic, not splitting into separate city-states, a pattern this file credits to Greece instead.

items.explain: The closing file states directly that Rome began as a kingdom, then threw out its own king and became a republic instead, led by two elected consuls along with a council called the Senate.  Each wrong choice claims an empire arrived immediately, a king stayed on in name only, or Rome split apart, none of which the file describes at this point.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that show Rome absorbing ideas directly from a civilization studied earlier in this record.
spans: Rome fought the rival city of Carthage across three long wars and won.
A road web linked it all, moving troops and officials fast across huge distances.
More years of civil war came next.
Rome also matched many of its own gods to Greek ones, treating each pair as one god under two names.
Rome took in Greek philosophy too.
items.explain: Closing the file, Rome is shown matching many of its own gods to Greek ones, treating each pair as one god under two names, and taking in Greek philosophy too, both direct callbacks to the civilization studied in an earlier case file.  The other sentences describe the wars against Carthage, Rome's road network, or its own civil war, none of which is an idea absorbed from an earlier civilization.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the case file closing on Rome.
choices: Rome lost all three of its long wars against Carthage.
Rome overthrew its own king and became a republic before later becoming an empire.
Rome matched many of its own gods to Greek ones, treating each pair as one god under two names.
Rome's location on a sea-facing peninsula pushed it steadily outward.
Rome kept citizenship limited to the city of Rome itself and never extended it.

distractorRationale.0: The passage says Rome fought Carthage across three long wars and won, not that Rome lost all three.
distractorRationale.4: The passage says Rome gave out citizenship widely across its conquered lands, a reach far past a narrow assembly limited to one city.

items.explain: The three correct details trace the closing file's own account: Rome's shift from kingdom to republic to empire, its matching of many of its own gods to Greek ones under new Roman names, and the peninsula geography that pushed its expansion outward.  The two wrong choices each invert what the passage actually says about the Punic Wars and about how widely Rome extended citizenship.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what ended Rome's nearly five-hundred-year-old republic?
choices: Julius Caesar's seizure of power, his assassination, and the civil war that followed, ending with his heir Octavian becoming emperor as Augustus.
A foreign invasion that conquered Rome and installed a new king from outside.
The Senate voluntarily handed power to Carthage after losing the wars against it.
Patrician and plebeian families united peacefully and voted to create an empire.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Rome fought the rival city of Carthage across three long wars and won.
His adopted heir, Octavian, rose as Rome's first emperor, taking the name Augustus.
Senators feared he wished to rule as a king, and they killed him.
A general named Julius Caesar seized power by force.

distractorRationale.1: Julius Caesar, the general who seized power, was Roman himself, not a foreign king; the passage never describes any outside invasion.
distractorRationale.2: The passage says Rome fought Carthage across three wars and won; Rome defeated Carthage, it did not hand power to it.
distractorRationale.3: The transition was violent, not peaceful: senators killed Caesar out of fear he wanted to be king, and years of civil war followed before Augustus became emperor.

items.explain: The passage traces the republic's end directly: Julius Caesar seized power by force, senators killed him fearing he wanted to rule as a king, and after more years of civil war his heir Octavian became Rome's first emperor, taking the name Augustus.  The other choices each invent a peaceful, foreign, or unrelated cause the passage does not describe.

items.stem: In eight words or fewer, name what the closing file says Rome did with citizenship that Athens never did.

extended it far past a narrow assembly

Any short phrasing naming that wider, conquered-lands reach, instead of Athens's narrower one-city model, earns credit here.

items.quote: For years afterward, rich patrician families held nearly all the real power.

Plebeian names the opposite, plainer class that fought for a share of that power, and consul names an elected office, not a whole family class, so neither term fits here.

partA.stem: The Recorder checks the Aegean Desk's own account one more time before closing the file.  According to that account, how far did Athenian democracy's real reach actually extend?

distractorRationale.3: Yohanan ben Zakkai belongs to an entirely different case file, on the Ancient Hebrews; the Han entry credits Zhang Qian, not him, with opening the Silk Road's western links.

partA.stem: According to the recovered entry, why does so much of the oldest written record come from Southern Mesopotamia in particular?
choices: Its scribes wrote on clay, a material tough enough to sit in a ruin and wait.
Its scribes cut their records into stone, which the plain had in large supply.
Its villages grew into cities, and cities are what create a need for records.
Its earliest tablets recorded counts of goods rather than poems or laws.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Scribes there wrote on wet clay tablets, and clay is stubborn.
The earliest tablets are not poems or laws at all.
Southern Mesopotamia had almost no stone and very little timber, but it had river mud without limit.
Villages had grown into cities, and cities needed records.

distractorRationale.2: Villages growing into cities explains why anyone needed records at all, a step every early civilization shared; it does not explain why this plain's records in particular are the ones that survived.
distractorRationale.3: What the tablets say is a separate question from why they lasted; receipts and poems written on the same clay would have survived a ruin equally well.

items.explain: The entry answers its own opening question directly: scribes on that plain wrote on wet clay, and clay is stubborn, so a tablet dropped in a ruin simply waits to be found.  Each wrong choice names a true detail from the entry, about stone, about cities, or about what the tablets say, that answers a different question than the one asked.

partA.stem: According to the recovered entry, what do the very earliest tablets from that plain actually record?

Plans for the stepped temple platforms the cities built.
Lists naming the patron god each city honored as its own.

The earliest tablets are not poems or laws at all.

distractorRationale.2: The stepped temple platform, the ziggurat, is in the entry and stood at the center of many of those cities, but the entry never describes a tablet holding a plan for one; the earliest tablets it names count grain, oil, and livestock.
distractorRationale.3: Each city did honor its own patron god, and the entry says so, but it never describes a tablet listing those gods; the tablets it describes count goods.

items.explain: The entry sets up the surprise on purpose: the earliest tablets are not poems or laws, they are receipts counting sacks of grain, jars of oil, and heads of livestock.  Each wrong choice borrows something else the entry mentions, a law code, a ziggurat, or patron gods, and puts it in the place the receipts actually hold.

The plain's palaces burned, and the tablets stored inside came out harder than they went in.

Palaces on that plain burned more than once, and the tablets stored inside came out of the ashes tougher than they went in.

distractorRationale.0: That describes the Sumerian cities BEFORE the conquest; the entry opens that same paragraph by saying no city on the plain stayed free forever.
distractorRationale.1: Babylon rose LATER in the entry's own sequence, after Akkad, so its king's law code is not what this conquest produced.
distractorRationale.3: Burned palaces are the entry's closing point about how the tablets survived at all; they are not a description of what changed politically when one ruler took the cities.

items.explain: The entry marks the shift plainly: separate Sumerian cities that had each run their own government were conquered and ruled from one capital at Akkad, which many historians call the first empire in the record.  The other choices each move a real detail, the cities before the conquest, Babylon's later rise, or the burned palaces, into a place the entry never puts it.

partA.stem: According to the briefing, what let people stop moving with the seasons and settle in one place?
choices: Towns eventually grew large enough to turn into the first cities.
Rivers flooded every year and spread fresh soil across the land nearby.
People lived in small bands and gathered whatever wild food they could find.
Farming produced more food than hunting and gathering had, so some people no longer had to search for their next meal.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: In Mesopotamia, the Tigris and the Euphrates flooded every year, spreading fresh soil across the land nearby.
For most of human history, people moved with the seasons, living in small bands and hunting and gathering wild food.
Farming grew more food than hunting ever had, and extra food let some people stop searching for their next meal.
Some towns grew large enough to become the first cities.

distractorRationale.0: Cities come several steps LATER in the briefing's own chain, after people had already settled and villages had grown into towns; they are a result of settling down, not its cause.
distractorRationale.1: Annual flooding is the briefing's answer to WHERE the first cities rose, the question it takes up next; it is not what let people stop moving in the first place.
distractorRationale.2: That describes the moving, foraging life the briefing says farming replaced, so it is the situation before the change rather than the cause of it.

items.explain: The briefing traces one clear chain: people planted seeds on purpose, farming grew more food than hunting ever had, and that extra food let some people stop searching for the next meal and settle instead.  Each wrong choice picks a stage that comes earlier or later in that same chain, or the river geography the briefing uses to answer a different question entirely.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the recovered entry on what the clay kept.
choices: A stepped temple platform called a ziggurat stood at the center of many early Sumerian cities.
Southern Mesopotamia had plenty of stone and timber, so its scribes rarely bothered with clay.
Metalworkers on that plain mixed copper with tin to make bronze.
Fire destroyed the clay tablets that were stored inside the plain's palaces.
The tablets show enslaved people standing at the top of the order, above kings and priests.
A ruler named Sargon conquered the Sumerian cities and ruled them from his own capital at Akkad.

distractorRationale.1: The entry says the reverse: that plain had almost no stone and very little timber, and river mud without limit, which is the whole reason clay became its writing material.
distractorRationale.3: Fire destroys most records, but the entry's favorite point is that fire BAKES clay harder, so tablets came out of burned palaces tougher than they went in.
distractorRationale.4: The tablets show kings and priests at the top and enslaved people at the bottom, many of them captives taken in war, so this choice turns the order upside down.

items.explain: All three correct details come straight from the entry: the ziggurat standing at the center of many Sumerian cities, the copper-and-tin mixture that made bronze, and Sargon's conquest of the Sumerian cities from his capital at Akkad.  The three wrong choices each invert something the entry actually says, about the plain's materials, about what fire did to clay, or about who stood where in the order the tablets record.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that explain how fire, which destroys most records, actually helped this one survive.
spans: Villages had grown into cities, and cities needed records.
Potters shaped clay on a turning wheel, and heavy carts rolled on wheels too.
No city on that plain stayed free forever.
Fire destroys most records, but fire bakes clay harder.
Palaces on that plain burned more than once, and the tablets stored inside came out of the ashes tougher than they went in.
items.explain: The entry turns the usual rule inside out: fire destroys most records, but fire bakes clay harder, so tablets stored in a burning palace came out of the ashes tougher than they went in.  The other three sentences describe why cities needed records at all, the tools of the age, or the loss of a city's freedom, none of which explains how the record survived.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state what the very earliest tablets from that plain actually record.
spans: Uruk and Ur each ran its own government, guarded its own walls, and honored its own patron god.
The earliest tablets are not poems or laws at all.
They are receipts, counting sacks of grain, jars of oil, and heads of livestock.
The tablets also show who stood where.
Metalworkers mixed copper with tin to make bronze, which held an edge far better than either metal alone.
items.explain: The entry says plainly what the earliest tablets are not, and then what they are: receipts counting sacks of grain, jars of oil, and heads of livestock.  The other sentences describe how the cities governed themselves, what the tablets reveal about social order, or the making of bronze, all true and all answering a different question.

items.stem: A stepped temple platform called a {{0}} stood at the center of many of them.

choices: pyramid
ziggurat
cuneiform

distractorRationale.0: A pyramid is the Egyptian tomb the record's Nile file describes, built because Egyptians believed a spirit needed a preserved body; the stepped platform at the center of a Sumerian city carries a different name.
distractorRationale.2: Cuneiform is the wedge-shaped writing Mesopotamian scribes pressed into wet clay with a cut reed, a script rather than a building.

items.quote: A stepped temple platform called a ziggurat stood at the center of many of them.
items.explain: The entry names the stepped temple platform standing at the center of many early Sumerian cities as a ziggurat.  A pyramid belongs to Egypt and its funerary beliefs, and cuneiform is a writing system rather than a structure, so neither restores the sentence.

items.stem: According to the recovered entry, why did the tablets stored inside the plain's palaces survive being burned?
choices: Scribes carried the tablets out of the palaces before the fires reached them.
The tablets were cut into stone, which fire cannot damage.
Fire bakes clay harder, so they came out of the ashes tougher than they went in.
The palaces were built of baked brick that kept the fires out.

distractorRationale.0: The entry never describes anyone rescuing tablets; it credits their survival to what fire does to clay, which is the opposite of a rescue.
distractorRationale.1: Stone is the one material that plain almost entirely lacked, and that shortage is exactly why its scribes wrote on river mud instead.
distractorRationale.3: Baked brick belongs to the Indus cities in a later file; this entry says the palaces burned more than once, and the burning is what hardened the tablets.

items.explain: The entry saves its favorite point for last: fire destroys most records, but fire bakes clay harder, so tablets stored in a palace that burned came out tougher than they went in.  Each wrong choice supplies a rescue, a material, or a building method the entry never claims, and one of them borrows from a different case file entirely.

items.stem: According to the recovered entry, why does the Provenance Office file the Code of Hammurabi as verified but unresolved?
choices: The stone is genuine, yet the code's opening promise and its actual clauses do not fully agree.
The stone the code was carved on has never been found.
Scholars cannot agree whether Hammurabi ruled Babylon at all.
The code covers house builders and merchants but leaves out farmers entirely.

distractorRationale.1: The entry states the stone still exists and that nothing in the file is a forgery, which is why the dispute is about meaning rather than authenticity.
distractorRationale.2: The entry gives Hammurabi's kingship at Babylon as plain background, and nothing in it treats that as a contested claim.
distractorRationale.3: The entry lists house builders, merchants and farmers together as groups the surviving clauses cover, so no group is missing from it.

items.explain: Verified and unresolved are two separate findings: the stone is real and the file says so plainly, while the gap between the code's promise of fair protection and clauses that punish by rank stays open.  Each wrong choice turns the unresolved half into a question about authenticity, about Hammurabi himself, or about coverage, none of which the entry disputes.

items.stem: According to the briefing, what is the one promise the Provenance Office keeps?
choices: Every claim is filed exactly as the first Recorder wrote it down.
The oldest case in the record is always the most reliable one.
Anything a conqueror recorded is treated as settled history.
No claim is filed as fact until the evidence proves it.

distractorRationale.0: The briefing says old claims drift, conquerors rewrite, rivals erase and forgers invent, which is precisely why a first writing is not treated as settled.
distractorRationale.1: The briefing sends a new Recorder to the oldest case to find where solid ground begins, which is a question about evidence rather than a promise about age.
distractorRationale.2: Conquerors rewriting the past to look better is one of the four ways the briefing says the record drifts, so their accounts get more scrutiny rather than less.

items.explain: The briefing opens with the promise the whole record runs on: nothing is filed as fact until evidence proves it, which is why the Office keeps checking claims that have drifted, been rewritten, been erased or been invented.  Each wrong choice replaces evidence with some other authority, whether the first writer, the oldest file, or the winner.

items.stem: Match each group of workers to the tool or method the recovered entry credits them with.
colLabels: Cut furrows with a plow instead of a digging stick
Shaped clay on a turning wheel
Mixed copper with tin to make bronze
items.explain: The entry credits each group with its own advance: potters shaped clay on a turning wheel, farmers cut furrows with a plow in place of a digging stick, and metalworkers mixed copper with tin to make bronze that held an edge better than either metal alone.  Sliding a tool one row up or down is exactly the confusion this table is built to catch.

partA.stem: According to the case file, why does the Office weigh the two carved stones so heavily?
choices: Each was made to praise its own king rather than to back up the Hebrew Bible, and each still names a king of Israel.
Both were carved by Israelite kings recording their own kingdom's history.
Together they settle which Assyrian king finished the siege of Samaria.
They give the reason the northern kingdom fell, calling it a punishment for abandoning the covenant.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Each was cut to praise its own king, which is exactly why the Office weighs it.
Those records do not fully agree about which king finished the siege, and the Office files that disagreement rather than smoothing it away.
It describes the defeat as a punishment for abandoning the covenant.
A carved stone known as the Mesha Stele was raised by a king of Moab.

distractorRationale.1: One stone was raised by a king of Moab and the other lists tribute paid to an Assyrian king; neither was made by an Israelite king writing his own history.
distractorRationale.2: The case file leaves that question open on purpose: the Assyrian records themselves do not fully agree about it, and the Office files the disagreement rather than smoothing it away.
distractorRationale.3: That explanation belongs to the account preserved in the Hebrew Bible, not to either stone, and the Office records it as the account's own reasoning.

items.explain: The case file explains its own method: a monument cut to praise a Moabite or Assyrian king had no reason to support the Hebrew Bible, and it names Israelite kings anyway, which is exactly what makes it useful outside evidence.  The other choices misplace who carved the stones, overstate what they settle, or hand the stones an explanation that belongs to the written account instead.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what happened to the northern kingdom of Israel?
choices: It outlasted the southern kingdom by a long stretch.
Assyria captured its capital, and Assyria's own royal records report that capture.
Its people became the ten lost tribes, which the record confirms as fact.
It kept the line of David along with the Temple in Jerusalem.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: In that account, the southern tribes kept the line of David and the Temple in Jerusalem, in a smaller kingdom called Judah.
Judah lasted longer than its northern neighbor did.
The Office files those stories as legend.
Assyrian armies took Samaria around seven hundred twenty-two BCE, and Assyrian royal records report the capture in their own words.

distractorRationale.0: The case file says the reverse: Judah, the southern kingdom, lasted longer than its northern neighbor did.
distractorRationale.2: Stories about ten lost tribes grew up much later, and the Office files them as legend rather than as anything the record confirms.
distractorRationale.3: The line of David and the Jerusalem Temple stayed with the SOUTHERN kingdom, Judah; the northern kingdom had its own capital at Samaria.

items.explain: The case file gives the northern kingdom's end in one line: Assyrian armies took Samaria, and Assyrian royal records report the capture in their own words, after which Assyria moved many of the defeated people elsewhere.  Each wrong choice swaps the two kingdoms, promotes a later legend to record, or hands the north something the file assigns to the south.

partA.stem: According to the case file, how does the Office handle the explanation the Hebrew Bible gives for the northern kingdom's fall?
choices: It files that explanation as the confirmed cause of the Assyrian conquest.
It throws the explanation out, because Assyrian records contradict it.
It records that explanation as the account's own reasoning rather than adopting it as a finding.
It treats the explanation as one of the later stories it files as legend.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The Office files those stories as legend.
That reasoning belongs to the account, and the Office records it as the account's own.
Those records do not fully agree about which king finished the siege, and the Office files that disagreement rather than smoothing it away.
The account preserved in the Hebrew Bible explains the fall in its own terms.

distractorRationale.0: The case file says the account explains the fall in its OWN terms, and explaining something in its own terms is not the same as the Office confirming a cause.
distractorRationale.1: The Assyrian records disagree with EACH OTHER about which king finished the siege; the file never says they contradict the account, and the Office never throws it out.
distractorRationale.3: The legend label belongs to the much later ten lost tribes stories at the end of the file, not to the account's own reasoning about the fall.

items.explain: The Office keeps a clean line here: the account preserved in the Hebrew Bible explains the fall as a punishment for abandoning the covenant, and the Office records that as the account's reasoning without adopting it, rejecting it, or calling it legend.  Each wrong choice collapses that line in a different direction, turning a recorded explanation into a confirmed cause, a refuted claim, or a story.

partA.stem: According to the case file on how the tradition survived, what should normally have become of a people in its position?
choices: It should have built its Temple a third time on the very same site.
It should have produced the longest file in the whole Office archive.
It should have shifted its center toward study, prayer, and law.
It should have blended into the peoples around it and stopped being a separate tradition.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: It did not rebuild either one.
This case file is the shortest one in the whole Office archive.
It should have faded into the peoples around it.
Now study, prayer, and law took that place, and any group could carry those things with it, anywhere.

distractorRationale.0: The case file says the tradition did NOT rebuild its state or its Temple; that is part of the surprise the file exists to check, not the expected outcome.
distractorRationale.1: The file's shortness is a fact about the file itself, not a prediction about the tradition, and the entry says that shortness is exactly what makes it worth checking closely.
distractorRationale.2: That shift is what actually happened at Yavneh and is why the tradition lasted; the file presents it as the surprising turn, not as the expected result.

items.explain: The file states its own expectation up front: a tradition with no king, no Temple, and no homeland should simply have faded into the peoples around it, and the record shows it did not.  Each wrong choice names something that actually happened, or a fact about the file's length, in place of the outcome the file predicted and then watched fail to arrive.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the case file on the kingdom that split in two.
choices: The Mesha Stele was raised by a king of Israel to record his own victories.
The Black Obelisk names Jehu, a later king of Israel, among those who paid tribute.
Assyrian royal records agree exactly on which king finished the siege of Samaria.
The southern kingdom, Judah, kept the line of David and the Temple in Jerusalem.
The Office files the ten lost tribes stories as verified record.
The Hebrew Bible describes Solomon's kingdom breaking apart soon after his death, around nine hundred thirty BCE.

distractorRationale.0: The Mesha Stele was raised by a king of Moab, and it names Omri of Israel as an enemy; an enemy's monument naming him is precisely what makes it useful as outside evidence.
distractorRationale.2: Those records do not fully agree on that point, and the case file says the Office files the disagreement rather than smoothing it away.
distractorRationale.4: The Office files those stories as legend; they grew up much later, and nothing in the entry treats them as anything the record verifies.

items.explain: The three correct details are the ones the case file supports directly: the Black Obelisk naming Jehu among those who paid tribute, Judah keeping the line of David and the Jerusalem Temple, and the split coming soon after Solomon died.  The three wrong choices each move a stone to the wrong maker, overstate how well the Assyrian records agree, or promote a later legend into the record.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that give the Office's reason for trusting two monuments raised by Israel's enemies.
spans: The Hebrew Bible describes Solomon's kingdom breaking apart soon after he died, around nine hundred thirty BCE.
A carved stone known as the Mesha Stele was raised by a king of Moab.
Neither stone was cut to prove the Hebrew Bible right.
Each was cut to praise its own king, which is exactly why the Office weighs it.
Assyrian armies took Samaria around seven hundred twenty-two BCE, and Assyrian royal records report the capture in their own words.
items.explain: The Office's reason is about motive: neither stone was cut to support the Hebrew Bible, each was cut to praise the king who raised it, and a monument that names Israel's kings anyway is worth more for exactly that reason.  The other sentences describe the split, name one of the stones, or report the fall of Samaria, all record and none of them the reason.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state what the account says caused the defeat and then hand that exact reasoning back to the account.
spans: The account preserved in the Hebrew Bible explains the fall in its own terms.
It describes the defeat as a punishment for abandoning the covenant.
That reasoning belongs to the account, and the Office records it as the account's own.
The Office files those stories as legend.
Judah lasted longer than its northern neighbor did.
items.explain: One sentence reports what the account says about the defeat, and the next hands that reasoning back to the account instead of adopting it, which is the whole method this file works by.  The other sentences introduce the account, file the much later lost-tribes stories as legend, or compare how long the two kingdoms lasted.

items.stem: The northern kingdom's capital came to be a city named {{0}}.

choices: Jerusalem
Samaria
Babylon

distractorRationale.0: Jerusalem stayed with the SOUTHERN kingdom, Judah, along with the line of David and the Temple; the northern kingdom of Israel had a capital of its own.
distractorRationale.2: Babylon is the Mesopotamian city whose king issued the law code filed at the very start of this record, and it was never a capital of either Israelite kingdom.

items.quote: The northern kingdom's capital came to be a city named Samaria.
items.explain: The case file gives the northern kingdom's capital as Samaria, the city Assyrian armies later took.  Jerusalem belongs to the southern kingdom in the same sentence pair, and Babylon belongs to an entirely different file, so neither one restores this sentence.

items.stem: According to the case file, which king does the Black Obelisk name among those who paid tribute to an Assyrian king?
choices: Omri, whom a Moabite king's stone names as an enemy.
Jehu, a later king of Israel.
Solomon, whose kingdom broke apart soon after he died.
David, whose line stayed with the southern kingdom.

distractorRationale.0: Omri is named on the OTHER monument, the Mesha Stele raised by a king of Moab, where he appears as an enemy who had pressed hard on Moab.
distractorRationale.2: Solomon belongs to the account of the split itself, generations before either monument was cut, and neither stone names him.
distractorRationale.3: The line of David stayed with Judah in the south, and the case file never places him on either of the two carved stones.

items.explain: The case file pairs each monument with the king it names: the Mesha Stele names Omri as an enemy of Moab, and the Black Obelisk names Jehu, a later king of Israel, among those who paid tribute.  Each wrong choice moves a real figure onto the wrong stone or into the wrong century, which is the confusion two outside monuments invite.

items.stem: According to the case file, how were the Israelites led after reaching Canaan but before they chose kings?
choices: By a single high priest based at the First Temple in Jerusalem.
By Moses, who kept leading them for the whole period after the Exodus.
By judges, called on only when trouble struck.
By Saul, the first of their kings, who ruled from the start.

distractorRationale.0: The First Temple was built by Solomon, generations after this period, so no Temple existed yet to base anyone at.
distractorRationale.1: The case file has Moses lead the people out of slavery and receive the law at Sinai, and it moves to judges only after the arrival in Canaan.
distractorRationale.3: Saul is named as the FIRST king, which is the change that ended the period of judges rather than a description of it.

items.explain: The case file gives the sequence plainly: after Canaan the Israelites were led by judges, called on only when trouble struck, and later chose kings instead, starting with Saul.  Each wrong choice pulls a figure or an institution from the wrong side of that change, whether the Temple, Moses, or the first king himself.

items.stem: According to the case file, who let the exiles return and build a Second Temple?
choices: Persian rulers, years after the Babylonian conquest.
The Babylonian army that had destroyed the first one.
Roman rulers, who later destroyed that Temple too.
Yohanan ben Zakkai, who opened a school at Yavneh.

distractorRationale.1: The Babylonian army is what destroyed the First Temple and forced the exile; the return came later and under different rulers.
distractorRationale.2: Rome enters the file much later, destroying the SECOND Temple during a revolt, so Roman rulers cannot be the ones who allowed it to be built.
distractorRationale.3: He got permission to open a school AFTER the Second Temple was already destroyed, and the file credits him with a shift in teaching rather than any rebuilding.

items.explain: The case file marks the turn clearly: years after the Babylonian conquest and exile, Persian rulers let the exiles return and build a Second Temple on the same site.  Each wrong choice names a power or a person from a different point in the same sequence, either the destroyer, the later destroyer, or the teacher who came after both.

items.stem: The case file traces the divided kingdom across five stages.  Put these five stages in the order they actually happened.
tiles: Omri rules in Israel, and a Moabite king's stone names him as an enemy
Assyrian armies take Samaria and move many of the defeated people elsewhere
In the account the Hebrew Bible preserves, Solomon dies and the kingdom breaks into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
Much later, stories grow up about ten lost tribes still wandering somewhere
Jehu rules later in Israel, and an Assyrian monument lists him among those paying tribute
items.explain: The case file fixes the sequence itself: the account the Hebrew Bible preserves has the kingdom splitting after Solomon, Omri then rules in Israel and turns up on a Moabite king's stone as an enemy, Jehu is named a LATER king of Israel, Assyrian armies take Samaria after that, and only much later do the lost-tribes stories grow up.  What fixes the middle of this order is the two KINGS rather than the two stones, because the entry dates neither stone and does say plainly that Jehu came later.

partA.stem: According to the case file, why does the Office refuse to describe one single Greek religion?
choices: There was no shared book and no shared creed, and what each city did varied from place to place.
Greek cities honored entirely different gods from one another, sharing no names at all.
No evidence about Greek worship survived for the Office to work from.
Greek worship happened only inside private households, never in public.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Many Greek cities honored the same gods under the same names.
Practice reached inside the house too.
Some of those calendars were carved into stone, and pieces of them survive.
There was no single Greek religion with one book and one creed.

distractorRationale.1: The case file says many Greek cities honored the SAME gods under the same names; the variation it describes is in what each city did, not in which gods they named.
distractorRationale.2: Evidence does survive, and the entry names its favorite kind: pieces of stone-carved offering calendars, working documents nobody wrote for a later reader.
distractorRationale.3: Household practice reached inside the house TOO, on top of the public processions, festivals, and games the entry has already described, so it was never the only setting.

items.explain: The case file opens by stating its limits: there was no single Greek religion with one book and one creed, many cities honored the same gods under the same names, and what each city actually did varied from place to place.  Each wrong choice pushes that carefulness too far in one direction, denying shared names, denying surviving evidence, or shrinking worship down to the household alone.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what makes the carved offering calendars the Office's favorite kind of evidence?
choices: They list which animal was owed to which god on which day.
They were working documents, written to do a job rather than to impress a later reader.
They record what worshippers believed the Pythia's answers meant.
They are the only Greek evidence that survives in stone at all.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Worshippers believed she spoke for the god.
Cities also kept calendars of offerings, listing which animal was owed to which god on which day.
That is the Office's favorite kind of evidence: a working document nobody wrote for posterity.
Stone pillars topped with a carved head stood at doorways and street corners in Athens, and people passing by honored them in small ways.

distractorRationale.0: That is what the calendars SAY, and it is accurate, but the entry credits their value to something else: they were working papers, not written for anyone later to read.
distractorRationale.2: Belief about the Pythia belongs to the Delphi section at the end of this entry; the calendars list offerings owed, not what anyone believed about an oracle.
distractorRationale.3: The entry describes other stone objects too, including carved pillars standing at Athenian doorways and street corners, so the calendars are not the only stone that survives.

items.explain: The Office prizes a document written for use rather than for an audience, and a city's carved list of which offering fell due on which day is exactly that: nobody wrote it for posterity, which is why it can be trusted about ordinary practice.  Each wrong choice trades that reason for the calendars' contents, for a different section of the entry, or for a claim about survival the entry never makes.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what happened to Athens in the year after the battle at Aegospotami?
choices: It rebuilt its navy with money supplied by Persia.
It signed a truce that was meant to end the fighting.
It surrendered, its long defensive walls came down, and thirty men were installed to rule it.
It beat a Spartan army on open ground and ended Spartan dominance.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Persia then paid for a Spartan fleet, and Spartan ships became a match for Athenian ones at last.
Its long defensive walls were pulled down, and a group of thirty men was installed to rule the city.
A truce called the Peace of Nicias, signed in four hundred twenty-one BCE, was supposed to end the fighting.
A Theban army beat a Spartan one at Leuctra in three hundred seventy-one BCE, and Spartan dominance ended there.

distractorRationale.0: Persia paid for a SPARTAN fleet, not an Athenian one, and that money is part of why Athens lost rather than a way it recovered.
distractorRationale.1: That truce came years earlier, in the middle of the war, and the entry says it held poorly and broke down; the war ended in a surrender, not a truce.
distractorRationale.3: A Theban army, not an Athenian one, ended Spartan dominance at Leuctra, and that happened decades after Athens had already surrendered.

items.explain: The case file gives the ending in sequence: Sparta destroyed the Athenian navy at Aegospotami, Athens surrendered the next year, its long walls were pulled down, and a group of thirty men was installed to rule the city.  Each wrong choice moves an event from a different year or a different city into that slot, which is exactly the confusion a long war invites.

partA.stem: According to the case file, what is the warning label the Office attaches to this war?
choices: The war's outcome is disputed, and no account agrees on who won it.
The sickness that struck Athens has never been identified.
No writer of the time recorded the war's final years at all.
Nearly all of what is known comes from one participant who had his own stake in the story.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Athens surrendered the next year.
He is a first-rate witness with a stake in the story.
His account also stops years before the war ends, so the last stretch comes from other writers.
Modern scholars still argue about what the disease actually was, so the Office files it as unidentified.

distractorRationale.0: The outcome is not in dispute in this entry: Athens surrendered, its walls came down, and the Office files the war itself as record.
distractorRationale.1: The unidentified sickness is filed as its own open question earlier in the entry; the warning label at the end is about who wrote the account, not about the disease.
distractorRationale.2: The main account does stop early, but the entry says the last stretch comes from other writers, so the final years are not unrecorded.

items.explain: The Office separates the war from the telling of it: the events are filed as record, while the fullest account comes from an Athenian general who fought in the war, lost a command, and wrote in exile, a first-rate witness with a stake in how the story reads.  Each wrong choice attaches the warning to the outcome, the disease, or a supposed gap in the record instead of to the witness.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the case file on the gods of the everyday.
choices: Athletes competed at Olympia in honor of Zeus, on ground that held his temple.
A priestess called the Pythia answered questions put to her at Delphi.
Greek plays were staged purely as entertainment, entirely apart from any religious festival.
Every Greek city followed one shared calendar of offerings, written down in a single book.
Households often kept a hearth fire burning in the home, with small offerings made there.

items.stem: According to the case file, how did the Greeks who gathered at Olympia understand the games there?

As a truce that let cities settle their quarrels.

partA.stem: According to the case file, why does the Office weigh the traveling monk's notebook so highly?

distractorRationale.2: Confucian teaching is the other school the earlier entry covers, and the Han later put it at the center of government; the Qin treated it as a threat rather than running on it.

items.quote: The school the Qin ran on is called Legalism.
items.explain: This entry exists to file the third school, the one the Qin state actually ran on, and names it Legalism.  Daoism and Confucian teaching are the two schools the Office's earlier entry on China already sets side by side, which is exactly why neither can fill this blank.

items.stem: According to the recovered entry, who carried Legalist ideas into the unified empire?
choices: A minister named Shang Yang, who rebuilt the state around those ideas.
A thinker named Han Fei, who set the argument out most fully.
A minister named Li Si.
An official named Zhang Heng, credited with an instrument for distant tremors.

distractorRationale.0: He rebuilt the Qin STATE around these ideas generations before the first emperor, so his work comes long before there was a unified empire to carry them into.
distractorRationale.1: The entry separates arguing from carrying on purpose: one man set the argument out most fully, and a different one took it into the government of the empire.
distractorRationale.3: He belongs to the Han part of the same entry, centuries later, and the credit attached to him concerns an instrument rather than a school of thought.

items.explain: The entry gives three men three different jobs: one rebuilt the Qin state around these ideas generations early, one set the argument out most fully, and a minister named Li Si later carried them into the unified empire.  Each wrong choice swaps one of those roles for another, or reaches into a different century of the same file.

items.stem: According to the case file, what did Han officials have to study?
choices: The Confucian classics, which the Qin had earlier tried to destroy.
The Legalist writings the Qin state had run on.
The Buddhist texts arriving along the trade routes.
The records of an official's journey west toward Central Asia.

distractorRationale.1: The Han put Confucian teaching at the center of government, and the case file makes what officials studied the mark of that reversal.
distractorRationale.2: Buddhism reached China slowly along those routes and took root beside Confucianism and Daoism, and the file never makes it a requirement for office.
distractorRationale.3: That journey is credited with opening the route's western links, a separate item in the same file, and nothing there makes it a subject of study.

items.explain: The case file makes the reading list the evidence: Han officials had to study the Confucian classics, the same texts the Qin had once tried to burn, and a person's grasp of them shaped who could serve the state.  Each wrong choice substitutes another body of writing from the same file, one of which the Han had explicitly moved away from.

items.stem: According to the case file, what did China's first emperor set one standard for?
choices: The teachings every school of thought was allowed to follow.
The route caravans were to take west toward Central Asia.
The number of rival states allowed to remain.
Writing, money, and weights across the whole empire.

distractorRationale.0: The case file describes him moving against ideas that threatened his power, which is suppression rather than a single standard for teaching.
distractorRationale.1: That trade web belongs to the Han dynasty in a later file, and later writers gave it the name Silk Road well after his reign.
distractorRationale.2: He beat every rival state rather than capping how many could remain, which is how he came to be China's first emperor at all.

items.explain: The case file lists the three things one system replaced: the empire's writing, its money, and its weights, in place of the many different ones the separate lands had used.  Each wrong choice takes a different action from his reign, or an achievement from a later dynasty, and calls it the standard he set.

items.stem: Match each part of the record to the turn the case file credits it with.
colLabels: Reached China slowly from India along the same routes silk traders used
Fell apart only a few years after its first emperor died
Put Confucian teaching at the very center of government
items.explain: The case file gives each one its own turn: the Qin fell apart within a few years of its first emperor's death, the Han put Confucian teaching at the center of government, and Buddhism arrived slowly from India along the trade routes rather than replacing what was already there.  Sliding a turn onto the neighboring row is exactly the confusion this table is built to catch.

partA.stem: According to the recovered entry, why is the Office able to file the execution itself as record?
choices: A Roman writer from outside the movement reports the same death under the same governor.
The movement's own followers taught that the teacher was the Messiah.
The letters a man named Paul wrote are the earliest Christian writings in the record.
Rome ruled the province through officials it sent out from the capital.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: His followers taught that he was the Messiah, a deliverer they found promised in their scriptures.
Rome ruled the province of Judea through officials it sent.
The earliest Christian writings in the record are letters, not stories about Jesus.
A Roman writer named Tacitus reports the same death under that governor.

distractorRationale.1: What followers taught is belief content, which the entry says the Office cannot check; the execution is filed as record because a writer outside the movement reports it.
distractorRationale.2: Those letters are the earliest Christian writings, and that matters for dating the movement, but the entry rests the execution on outside reporting rather than on the letters.
distractorRationale.3: Roman rule of the province is the setting the entry establishes first, which is how there was a Roman governor at all; it is not the reason the death can be filed as record.

items.explain: The entry draws its line where the evidence changes: a Roman writer with no connection to the movement reports the same death under the same governor, so the execution is filed as record, while what people believed about that teacher is filed only as what they believed.  Each wrong choice offers belief content, a dating point, or the political setting in place of the outside report the Office actually rests on.

partA.stem: Closing the file, the Recorder reopens the long war between Athens and Sparta.  According to that entry, why does the Office attach a warning label to what is known about it?
choices: The years the war ran are disputed among modern scholars.
Much of it traces back to a single participant who had his own stake in the story.
Persia's payment for a Spartan fleet was never confirmed.
The Office could not decide which side started the fighting.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Persia then paid for a Spartan fleet, and Spartan ships became a match for Athenian ones at last.
Athens and Sparta fought for twenty-seven years, from four hundred thirty-one to four hundred four BCE.
Much of what is known about it traces back to one man.
The Office files the war as record and the telling as evidence with an interest attached.

distractorRationale.0: The entry gives the war's span as settled record; what modern scholars still argue over there is the sickness that struck Athens, not the years of the war.
distractorRationale.2: The entry states that payment as record, and treats it as part of why Spartan ships became a match for Athenian ones; nothing there calls it unconfirmed.
distractorRationale.3: The Office's stated position is about the TELLING, filed as evidence with an interest attached; that entry never raises a question about who started the war.

items.explain: That entry keeps two things apart, and the capstone borrows the habit: the war itself is filed as record, while the fullest account of it came from an Athenian general who fought in it, lost a command, and wrote in exile with a stake in how it reads.  Each wrong choice attaches the warning to the dates, to a payment, or to a dispute that entry never opens.

partA.stem: Before closing the file, the Recorder checks the entry on a visitor's notes and a number that traveled.  According to that entry, what did the Office correct about the ten digits most of the world writes with?
choices: They were invented by a scholar born in four hundred seventy-six CE.
Their value comes from a visitor with no stake in a ruler's reputation.
Their usual name credits the scholars who carried them west instead of the ones who built them.
Their symbols had no way at all to mark an empty place.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A scholar named Aryabhata, born in four hundred seventy-six CE, wrote a short book on astronomy and mathematics.
The name credits the messenger and skips the sender.
An outside witness with no stake in a ruler's reputation is rare in this record, and the Office weighs him accordingly.
A symbol for zero held the empty place.

distractorRationale.0: That birth year belongs to Aryabhata, whom the entry credits with a short book on astronomy and mathematics; the entry says the number system matters more than any single scholar.
distractorRationale.1: The no-stake witness is that entry's OTHER anchor, the traveling monk's notebook, filed alongside the number system rather than as part of it.
distractorRationale.3: The entry says a symbol for zero held the empty place, so the system did mark it, and that symbol is part of what makes the system work.

items.explain: The capstone reaches back for the cleanest example of a name that drifted: the ten digits were built by Indian mathematicians, carried west by Arabic-speaking scholars, and then named for the carriers, so the usual name credits the messenger and skips the sender.  Each wrong choice picks a different piece of that entry, its named scholar, its other anchor, or its zero, and puts it where the correction belongs.

partA.stem: Closing the file, the Recorder returns to the entry on China's third school.  According to that entry, why should cheap writing material matter to a Recorder at all?
choices: It proves one court official invented paper entirely on his own.
It shows that Legalist habits stayed inside Han law.
It explains why the dynasty came apart around two hundred twenty CE.
It changes what gets written down and copied, so the record after it runs thicker.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Scraps of older paper have turned up since, so the craft was already in use before he improved it.
Cheap writing material changes what gets written down and what gets copied.
The dynasty itself came apart around two hundred twenty CE, worn down by revolts, court struggles, and generals who stopped listening.
Han law kept much of the same machinery, and later dynasties kept it too.

distractorRationale.0: That entry qualifies the credit directly: older scraps have turned up since, so the craft was already in use before the official improved it.
distractorRationale.1: Legalist habits surviving in Han law is a separate finding earlier in that entry, about how a government ran rather than about what the record preserves.
distractorRationale.2: That entry credits the dynasty's collapse to revolts, court struggles, and generals who stopped listening, with no connection at all to writing material.

items.explain: The capstone reaches back for the point a Recorder cares about most: what survives depends on what people wrote on, so a cheaper material means more gets written down and copied and the record after it runs thicker.  Each wrong choice takes a real finding from that same entry, about a credit, about Legalist habits, or about a dynasty's fall, and answers a question it was not built to answer.

items.stem: Choose the three details that are true, according to the addendum on Rome's long ending.
choices: The eastern half of the empire fell within a hundred years of the western half.
Later writers named the two quieter centuries after Augustus the Pax Romana.
The empire was divided into a western half and an eastern half in three hundred ninety-five CE.
The eastern empire's own people called their state Byzantine.
Roman coins carried more and more silver as the two hundreds CE went on.
In four hundred seventy-six CE a commander removed the last emperor the west still had.

distractorRationale.0: The addendum says the eastern half did not fall then: ruled from Constantinople, it lasted nearly another thousand years.
distractorRationale.3: Its own people called themselves Romans, in Greek; Byzantine is a label European scholars applied much later, and the addendum says its own people never used it.
distractorRationale.4: The addendum says coins carried less and less silver while prices climbed, which is part of why the empire nearly came apart in those years.

items.explain: The three correct details track the addendum's own sequence: later writers named the quiet stretch the Pax Romana, the empire was divided into two halves in that year, and a commander removed the west's last emperor without replacing him.  The three wrong choices each reverse something the addendum is careful about, the eastern half's survival, the name its own people used, and which way the silver in the coins was going.

items.stem: This entry files a teacher named Jesus under one strict rule.  Tap the two sentences that state that rule, and what that rule still lets the Office file.
spans: A Recorder records what people believed, never a belief as a fact.
The method was crucifixion, a Roman way of killing.
His followers taught that he was the Messiah, a deliverer they found promised in their scriptures.
What it files is that people held these beliefs, and held them early.
Nero punished believers in the city of Rome after a fire there, in sixty-four CE.
items.explain: The rule and its result are stated in two places: a Recorder records what people believed and never files a belief as a fact, and what the Office can still file is that people held those beliefs, and held them early.  The other sentences report the method of execution, what followers taught, and one episode of official punishment, each of which the rule is then applied to.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that say what the toleration order did not do and when Christianity actually became the empire's religion.
spans: Roman officials moved against the movement at times, but not steadily, and rarely everywhere.
In three hundred thirteen CE, Constantine and a fellow emperor granted freedom of worship to every religion, not to one.
That order did not make Christianity the empire's religion, whatever later accounts say.
Theodosius did that in three hundred eighty CE.
Maybe one person in ten in the empire had joined by three hundred CE, maybe far fewer.
items.explain: The correction runs across two sentences: the order of three hundred thirteen did NOT make Christianity the empire's religion, and a later emperor did that almost seventy years afterward.  The other sentences describe episodic official pressure, the toleration order itself, and how small a share of the empire had joined by three hundred.

items.stem: The earliest Christian writings in the record are {{0}}, not stories about Jesus.

choices: poems
laws
letters

distractorRationale.0: The long poems in this record are the two Indian epics filed in another entry, copied and recited across centuries; the earliest Christian writings named here take a different form.
distractorRationale.1: A law code is what the record's very first file holds, carved in stone under a Babylonian king, and the entry never describes the earliest Christian writings as laws.

items.quote: The earliest Christian writings in the record are letters, not stories about Jesus.
items.explain: The entry makes a point of the form: the earliest Christian writings in the record are letters written to small groups, not stories about Jesus, which is what makes them the closest written evidence to the events.  Poems and laws each belong to other files in this record, so neither restores the sentence.

items.stem: Closing the file, the Recorder checks the record's Nile entry one more time.  According to that entry, what did cuneiform and hieroglyphs both manage to do?
choices: They used the same wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay.
They let a record outlive the person who made it.
They were both carved onto papyrus and stone by Egyptian scribes.
They recorded only the achievements of pharaohs and kings.

distractorRationale.0: Wedge-shaped marks in wet clay describe cuneiform alone; the entry gives hieroglyphs a separate method, drawn or carved onto papyrus and stone.
distractorRationale.2: Papyrus and stone are what EGYPTIAN scribes used, and the entry credits cuneiform to Mesopotamian scribes working in clay instead.
distractorRationale.3: The entry never narrows either system to royal achievements, and the record's first file describes tablets counting grain, oil and livestock.

items.explain: The Nile entry ends by saying what the two systems shared despite their different methods: both let a record live on long after its maker was gone.  Each wrong choice takes one system's method and hands it to both, or narrows what either was used for in a way that entry never does.

items.stem: Before closing the file, the Recorder rereads the record's shortest entry.  According to that entry, what did the tradition prove by NOT rebuilding its state or its Temple?
choices: That a third Temple had been built somewhere else instead.
That the diaspora ended and the exiles all returned home.
That it had never truly leaned on either one alone.
That Rome had allowed the old kingdom to be restored.

distractorRationale.0: The entry says the tradition did not rebuild either one, and it names no third Temple anywhere; the survival is what happened in place of rebuilding.
distractorRationale.1: The diaspora is described as growing as more people scattered further, and the entry never has it end.
distractorRationale.3: Rome had already crushed the state and then destroyed the Second Temple, which is the loss the entry says should have finished the tradition.

items.explain: The shortest entry closes on exactly this claim: the tradition outlived its own state and its own Temple, did not rebuild either one, and proved instead that it had never truly leaned on them alone.  Each wrong choice supplies a restoration the entry rules out, whether a new Temple, a return, or a kingdom given back.

items.stem: According to the recovered entry, how far had the movement spread inside the empire by the year three hundred?
choices: Most of the empire had joined by then.
It had not yet spread beyond the province of Judea.
Only the city of Rome had communities of believers.
Maybe one person in ten, and maybe far fewer.

distractorRationale.0: The entry bounds the pace deliberately: growth was steady rather than sudden, and it puts the share at maybe one person in ten by that year, maybe far fewer.
distractorRationale.1: The entry describes it moving along Rome's roads and sea lanes into cities across the empire long before that year, so it had reached far past one province.
distractorRationale.2: Believers are described in the city of Rome and in cities across the empire, and letters were written to small groups in the eastern empire decades earlier.

items.explain: The entry attaches a bound to the spread claim in the same paragraph that makes it: the movement traveled along Rome's roads and sea lanes, a shared Greek language helped, growth was steady rather than sudden, and maybe one person in ten inside the empire had joined by that year, maybe far fewer.  Each wrong choice drops the bound, either overstating the reach or shrinking it to a single province or city.

items.stem: In eight words or fewer, name the label European scholars later gave the eastern empire, which its own people never used.
items.explain: The addendum closes the whole record on a name applied by whoever wrote last: the eastern empire's own people called themselves Romans, in Greek, and much later European scholars began calling that empire Byzantine, a name its own people never used for their empire.  Any short phrasing naming that later label earns credit here.
